nodes.label: Scientific models and theories develop over time with new data
nodes.objective: Explain how new experimental data can lead to changes in scientific models or theories.
essentialPoints: Scientific theories are provisional and change when new evidence is found
New data can support, refine or overturn existing models
Deciding whether given data supports a theory is a testable skill

nodes.label: Independent, dependent and control variables
nodes.objective: Identify and explain the role of independent, dependent and control variables in an investigation.
essentialPoints: The independent variable is the one changed or selected by the investigator
The dependent variable is measured for each change in the independent variable
Control variables are kept constant to ensure a fair test

nodes.label: Constructing and interpreting frequency tables, bar charts and histograms
nodes.objective: Construct and interpret frequency tables, bar charts and histograms from data.
essentialPoints: Frequency tables organise raw data into categories or intervals
Bar charts and histograms are used to display and interpret this data visually

nodes.label: Using scientific vocabulary, terminology and definitions
nodes.objective: Use correct scientific vocabulary, terminology and definitions when communicating chemistry.
essentialPoints: Correct scientific terms must be used precisely rather than everyday synonyms
Definitions of key terms must be stated accurately

nodes.label: Recognising and using decimal form
nodes.objective: Recognise and use expressions in decimal form in calculations and measurements.
essentialPoints: Decimal numbers represent quantities that are not whole numbers
Decimal place value determines precision of a measurement or calculation

nodes.label: Using ratios, fractions and percentages
nodes.objective: Use ratios, fractions and percentages to solve numerical problems in chemistry contexts.
essentialPoints: Ratios compare quantities relative to each other
Fractions and percentages express a part relative to a whole

nodes.label: Understanding and using algebraic/mathematical symbols
nodes.objective: Understand and use the symbols =, <, <<, >>, >, ∝ and ~ correctly in scientific contexts.
essentialPoints: Each symbol has a precise mathematical meaning (equals, less than, much less than, much greater than, greater than, proportional to, approximately equal to)
Correct use of these symbols is required when expressing relationships between quantities

nodes.label: Understanding y = mx + c as a linear relationship
nodes.objective: Understand that y = mx + c represents a linear relationship between two variables.
essentialPoints: m represents the gradient of the line and c represents the y-intercept
A linear relationship produces a straight-line graph

nodes.label: Visualising and representing 2D and 3D forms
nodes.objective: Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms, including 2D representations of 3D objects such as molecular structures.
essentialPoints: 3D structures (e.g. molecules, crystal lattices) can be represented in 2D diagrams
Interpreting 2D representations requires visualising the true 3D shape

nodes.label: Taking timed readings at fixed intervals
nodes.objective: Take measurements at regular, fixed time intervals during a reaction to monitor how a variable changes over time.
essentialPoints: Consistent, regular time intervals allow rate of change to be tracked and compared fairly
A stopwatch or timer is started at a defined starting point (e.g. mixing of reagents)

nodes.label: Atoms and elements
nodes.objective: State that all substances are made of atoms and define an atom and an element.
essentialPoints: An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist
An element consists of only one type of atom
There are about 100 different elements, shown in the periodic table

nodes.label: Electron shell arrangement and outer shell electrons
nodes.objective: Recall that atoms have electrons arranged in shells and that the outer shell electrons determine bonding behaviour.
essentialPoints: Electrons occupy shells around the nucleus
The outer (highest) shell electrons are involved in bonding
Group number relates to number of outer shell electrons

nodes.label: Simple particle model of solid, liquid and gas states
nodes.objective: Describe the three states of matter using the simple particle model (particles as solid spheres).
essentialPoints: Three states: solid, liquid, gas
Particles represented as small solid spheres
Arrangement/movement of spheres differs between states

nodes.label: Nanoscience size range (1-100 nm) compared to fine (PM2.5) and coarse (PM10) particles
nodes.objective: State the size range of nanoparticles (1-100 nm) and compare this to fine particles (PM2.5) and coarse particles (PM10).
essentialPoints: Nanoparticles are 1-100 nm in size (a few hundred atoms)
Fine particles (PM2.5) have diameters 100-2500 nm
Coarse particles (PM10, dust) have diameters 2.5x10^-6 to 1x10^-5 m

externalPrerequisites.prerequisiteConcept: Standard form and order of magnitude calculations (Topic 0)

nodes.label: Surface area to volume ratio increases by factor of 10 as cube side decreases by factor of 10
nodes.objective: Calculate how surface area to volume ratio changes as the size of a cube decreases, showing the ratio increases by a factor of 10 when the side decreases by a factor of 10.
essentialPoints: Surface area to volume ratio = surface area / volume
As cube side length decreases by factor of 10, SA:V ratio increases by factor of 10

externalPrerequisites.prerequisiteConcept: Surface area and volume of cubes (Topic 0 maths skills)

nodes.label: Changing the subject of an equation
nodes.objective: Rearrange algebraic equations to make a required quantity the subject.
essentialPoints: An equation can be rearranged to solve for any variable within it
Substituting values requires correct units

nodes.label: Using ratios, fractions and percentages
nodes.objective: Apply ratio, fraction and percentage calculations to chemical quantities.
essentialPoints: Ratios express relative proportions of quantities
Percentages express a part as a proportion of 100

nodes.label: Using apparatus to measure mass, time, temperature and volume accurately
nodes.objective: Use appropriate apparatus to make and record accurate measurements of mass, time, temperature and volume of liquids and gases.
essentialPoints: Select apparatus appropriate to the precision required
Read scales correctly (e.g. avoiding parallax error)

nodes.label: Law of conservation of mass
nodes.objective: State that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction, so mass of products equals mass of reactants.
essentialPoints: No atoms are created or destroyed in a chemical reaction
Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products in a closed system

nodes.label: Ions form by loss/gain of electrons giving charged particles
nodes.objective: State that ions are charged particles formed by electron loss or gain.
essentialPoints: Atoms lose or gain electrons to form ions
Losing electrons gives positive ions, gaining gives negative ions

nodes.label: Deriving formulae of ionic compounds from ion charges
nodes.objective: Balance charges of common ions to write correct ionic formulae.
essentialPoints: Total positive charge must equal total negative charge
Use ratios of ions to balance overall charge

nodes.label: Balancing symbol equations
nodes.objective: Balance atoms on both sides of a chemical equation.
essentialPoints: Same number of each atom on both sides
Use coefficients not subscripts to balance

nodes.label: Moles and concentration (mol/dm3)
nodes.objective: Calculate concentration in mol/dm3 using moles and volume.
essentialPoints: concentration = moles / volume(dm3)
Rearrange to find any one variable

nodes.label: Using an appropriate number of significant figures
nodes.objective: Report calculated answers to a sensible number of significant figures.
essentialPoints: Match sig figs to precision of data given
Avoid over/under-precision in final answers

nodes.label: Calculating arithmetic mean from repeated measurements
nodes.objective: Calculate the mean of a set of repeated measurements.
essentialPoints: Sum values and divide by number of readings
Used to reduce impact of random error

nodes.label: Safe use of a Bunsen burner and heating devices
nodes.objective: Use a Bunsen burner and water bath/electric heater safely for heating.
essentialPoints: Use blue flame for heating, yellow (safety) flame when not in direct use
Water bath/electric heater used for gentler, controlled heating

nodes.label: Filtration technique
nodes.objective: Separate an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper and funnel.
essentialPoints: Pour mixture through filter paper in funnel
Residue stays on paper, filtrate passes through

nodes.label: Evaporation and crystallisation technique
nodes.objective: Evaporate solvent from a solution to grow salt crystals.
essentialPoints: Gently heat/evaporate solution to point of saturation
Leave to cool and crystallise, then filter and dry crystals

nodes.label: Using a burette and pipette to measure liquid volumes accurately
nodes.objective: Read burette/pipette volumes accurately including reading the meniscus.
essentialPoints: Read meniscus at eye level to the correct graduation
Burette delivers variable measured volume; pipette delivers fixed volume

nodes.label: Using an indicator to detect a titration endpoint colour change
nodes.objective: Identify the colour change of an indicator that signals the endpoint of a titration.
essentialPoints: Indicator changes colour sharply at the point of exact neutralisation
Different indicators used depending on acid/alkali combination

nodes.label: Collecting and measuring the volume of a gas produced
nodes.objective: Use gas syringe or displacement of water to measure gas volume produced in a reaction.
essentialPoints: Gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder collects gas over time
Volume readings taken at set time intervals

nodes.label: Using a thermometer to measure temperature accurately
nodes.objective: Read and record temperature to appropriate precision using a thermometer.
essentialPoints: Read scale at eye level to avoid parallax error
Record to nearest suitable graduation
Allow reading to stabilise before recording

nodes.label: Identifying independent, dependent and control variables
nodes.objective: Distinguish the variable changed, the variable measured, and variables kept constant in an investigation.
essentialPoints: Independent variable is deliberately changed
Dependent variable is measured as the outcome
Control variables are kept constant to ensure a fair test

nodes.label: Calculating an arithmetic mean from repeated readings
nodes.objective: Calculate the mean of a set of repeated measurements, excluding anomalies.
essentialPoints: Identify and exclude anomalous results
Sum remaining values and divide by number of readings

nodes.label: Plotting two variables from experimental data on a graph
nodes.objective: Plot experimental data correctly with labelled axes, suitable scales, and best-fit line/curve.
essentialPoints: Choose sensible scales covering the data range
Plot points accurately and label axes with units
Draw line or curve of best fit

nodes.label: Particle collision model of reactions
nodes.objective: Explain that reactions occur when particles collide with sufficient energy and correct orientation.
essentialPoints: Particles must collide to react
Only collisions with enough energy result in a reaction
This underlies rate of reaction and activation energy ideas

nodes.label: Writing half equations for electrode reactions
nodes.objective: Write balanced half equations showing electron loss or gain at an electrode.
essentialPoints: Half equations show oxidation (electron loss) or reduction (electron gain) separately
Must be balanced for atoms and charge
Electrons shown explicitly as e-

nodes.label: Moles and concentration calculations (mol/dm3)
nodes.objective: Calculate amount in moles and concentration in mol/dm3 and g/dm3.
essentialPoints: moles = concentration x volume
concentration in mol/dm3 converted to g/dm3 using molar mass

nodes.label: Conservation of energy in chemical reactions
nodes.objective: State that energy is conserved overall in a chemical reaction.
essentialPoints: Total energy in the universe is unchanged by a reaction
Energy is transferred between reacting system and surroundings, not created or destroyed

nodes.label: Bond breaking requires energy input (HT)
nodes.objective: State that energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants.
essentialPoints: Breaking a chemical bond requires an input of energy
This energy input corresponds to bond energy of that bond

nodes.label: Bond forming releases energy (HT)
nodes.objective: State that energy is released when new bonds are formed in the products.
essentialPoints: Forming a chemical bond releases energy
This energy release corresponds to the bond energy of that bond

nodes.label: Simple cell: definition and construction
nodes.objective: Describe how a simple cell is made from two different metals in contact with an electrolyte, producing a voltage.
essentialPoints: A simple cell consists of two different metal electrodes in an electrolyte
A voltage is produced between the two electrodes
Chemicals in the cell react to produce electricity

nodes.label: Drawing a tangent to a curve and finding its gradient
nodes.objective: Draw a tangent to a point on a curved graph and calculate its gradient as a measure of instantaneous rate.
essentialPoints: A tangent is a straight line touching a curve at one point without crossing it
Gradient = change in y / change in x using two points on the tangent line
Used to find rate of change at a specific instant rather than mean rate

nodes.label: Plotting and interpreting graphs from experimental data
nodes.objective: Plot two variables from experimental data and interpret the resulting graph shape.
essentialPoints: Independent variable on x-axis, dependent variable on y-axis
Choose sensible scales and plot points accurately
Interpret trends, curves and straight lines in terms of the relationship between variables

nodes.label: Using significant figures and calculating arithmetic means
nodes.objective: Process repeated measurement data using appropriate significant figures and calculate a mean.
essentialPoints: Mean = sum of readings / number of readings, excluding anomalies
Report calculated values to an appropriate number of significant figures

nodes.label: Measuring gas volume produced using a gas syringe or displacement of water
nodes.objective: Use appropriate apparatus to measure the volume of gas produced during a reaction over time.
essentialPoints: A gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder over water can measure volume of gas collected
Volume readings are taken at set time intervals to build a rate dataset

nodes.label: Timing a colour change or turbidity change (e.g. disappearing cross method)
nodes.objective: Use a stopwatch to time how long it takes for a solution to become opaque or change colour, viewed against a marked cross or colour standard.
essentialPoints: Start timer when reactants are mixed and stop when a mark viewed through the solution disappears or a colour change is judged complete
Consistent judging position and lighting reduce subjective error

nodes.label: Particles in motion and collisions between reacting particles
nodes.objective: State that particles in solutions and gases move randomly and can collide with each other.
essentialPoints: Particles in liquids and gases move constantly and randomly
A chemical reaction requires particles of reactants to collide

nodes.label: Reversible reactions and the reversible arrow notation
nodes.objective: Describe reversible reactions as ones in which the products can react to re-form the original reactants, represented using the ⇌ symbol.
essentialPoints: In a reversible reaction, products of the forward reaction can react to reform the original reactants
This is represented A + B ⇌ C + D
The direction of a reversible reaction can be changed by changing the reaction conditions

nodes.label: Exothermic and endothermic reactions (recap for reversible context)
nodes.objective: Recall that exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings and endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings.
essentialPoints: An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, often shown by a temperature rise
An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, often shown by a temperature fall

nodes.label: Carbon forms chains and rings via C-C bonds enabling organic diversity
nodes.objective: Explain why carbon can form a huge variety of compounds through chains and rings of C-C bonds.
essentialPoints: Carbon atoms can bond to other carbon atoms forming chains and rings
This gives rise to a very large variety of possible carbon compounds
Organic chemistry is the study of these carbon compounds

nodes.label: Using an appropriate number of significant figures in calculations and answers
nodes.objective: Round and report numerical answers to an appropriate number of significant figures.
essentialPoints: Significant figures indicate precision of a measurement or calculation
Answers should not be given to more sig figs than the least precise data used

nodes.label: Using ratios, fractions, decimals and percentages in calculations
nodes.objective: Manipulate ratios, fractions, decimals and percentages within scientific calculations.
essentialPoints: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind
Fractions, decimals and percentages are interchangeable representations of a proportion

nodes.label: Plotting and reading data from graphs (axes, scales, line of best fit)
nodes.objective: Plot experimental data accurately on labelled axes and draw an appropriate line/curve of best fit.
essentialPoints: Choose sensible scales that use most of the graph paper
Plot points accurately and draw a line/curve of best fit
Read values from a graph by interpolation

nodes.label: Safe use of a Bunsen burner and water bath/electric heater for heating
nodes.objective: Use a Bunsen burner and water bath/electric heater safely to heat substances.
essentialPoints: Bunsen burner used for direct strong heating; water bath for gentler, controlled heating
Safety precautions include using a heatproof mat and appropriate flame settings

nodes.label: Filtration technique to separate an insoluble solid from a liquid
nodes.objective: Use filter paper and funnel to separate a solid residue from a liquid filtrate.
essentialPoints: Filter paper allows liquid (filtrate) through but retains the insoluble solid (residue)

nodes.label: Evaporation and crystallisation technique to obtain solid crystals from solution
nodes.objective: Evaporate a solution to the point of saturation and allow crystals to form on cooling.
essentialPoints: Gentle heating evaporates solvent until saturation point is reached
Slow cooling allows crystals of the dissolved solute to form

nodes.label: Titration technique: using a burette, pipette and indicator to find an accurate end point
nodes.objective: Carry out an acid-base titration accurately using a pipette to measure a fixed volume and a burette to add the other solution dropwise to a colour-change end point.
essentialPoints: Pipette delivers an accurate fixed volume of one solution into a flask
Burette delivers the second solution gradually, reading the volume added at the meniscus
Indicator signals the end point by a sharp colour change
Repeat titrations until concordant results are obtained

nodes.label: Measuring the volume of gas produced using a gas syringe or displacement of water
nodes.objective: Collect and measure the volume of a gas produced in a reaction using appropriate apparatus.
essentialPoints: A gas syringe measures gas volume directly as the plunger is pushed out
Downward displacement of water can be used for gases insoluble in water

nodes.label: Measuring temperature change accurately using a thermometer in reacting solutions
nodes.objective: Measure and record the temperature of a reacting mixture accurately over time.
essentialPoints: Thermometer should be read at eye level to avoid parallax error
Insulation (e.g. polystyrene cup) reduces heat loss to surroundings

nodes.label: Simple distillation technique to separate a solvent from a solution
nodes.objective: Use simple distillation apparatus to separate and collect a pure solvent from a solution by evaporation and condensation.
essentialPoints: Heating the solution evaporates the more volatile component
Condenser cools the vapour back into a liquid collected separately from the residue

nodes.label: Measuring pH using indicators, pH paper or a pH probe
nodes.objective: Determine the pH of a solution using an appropriate method and equipment.
essentialPoints: Universal indicator or pH paper gives an approximate pH via colour comparison
A calibrated pH probe/meter gives a more precise numerical reading

nodes.label: Pure substances: definition (single element or compound, not mixed)
nodes.objective: Define a pure substance in the chemical sense as a single element or compound not mixed with any other substance.
essentialPoints: A pure substance in chemistry is a single element or compound
This differs from the everyday meaning of 'pure' (e.g. unadulterated, natural)

nodes.label: Chromatography principle: stationary and mobile phases, separation by distribution
nodes.objective: Explain how paper chromatography separates mixtures based on differing distribution of substances between stationary and mobile phases.
essentialPoints: Chromatography has a stationary phase (paper) and a mobile phase (solvent)
Different substances distribute differently between the two phases, causing them to separate as the solvent moves
Substances that are more soluble/attracted to the mobile phase travel further

nodes.label: Writing balanced symbol equations (background)
nodes.objective: Write balanced symbol equations for chemical reactions.
essentialPoints: Equations must have equal numbers of each atom on both sides
State symbols show the physical state of each substance

nodes.label: Testing metal ions with sodium hydroxide solution: procedure (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Add sodium hydroxide solution dropwise to a metal ion solution and observe the precipitate formed.
essentialPoints: Sodium hydroxide solution is added dropwise, then in excess, to the unknown solution
The colour and solubility-in-excess of any precipitate formed is observed

nodes.label: Testing for halide ions using silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid: procedure (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution to a solution to test for halide ions.
essentialPoints: Dilute nitric acid is added first to remove interference from other ions (e.g. carbonates)
Silver nitrate solution is then added and any precipitate observed

nodes.label: Testing for sulfate ions using barium chloride and dilute hydrochloric acid: procedure (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Add dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride solution to a solution to test for sulfate ions.
essentialPoints: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added first to remove interference from other ions (e.g. carbonates)
Barium chloride solution is then added and any precipitate observed

nodes.label: Instrumental methods of analysis: accurate, sensitive, rapid (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: State that instrumental methods are used to detect and identify elements and compounds and describe their general characteristics.
essentialPoints: Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid
They are used by forensic and drug-control scientists among others

nodes.label: Early Earth's atmosphere formed by intense volcanic activity
nodes.objective: Describe the theory that volcanic activity in Earth's first billion years released gases forming the early atmosphere and water vapour that condensed to form the oceans.
essentialPoints: Intense volcanic activity during first billion years released gases
Early atmosphere likely mainly CO2 with little/no oxygen, similar to Mars/Venus today
Water vapour released condensed to form the oceans
Volcanoes also released nitrogen (built up gradually) and small proportions of methane and ammonia

nodes.label: Photosynthesis equation and its role in producing oxygen
nodes.objective: State the word/symbol equation for photosynthesis and describe how algae and plants produced atmospheric oxygen over time.
essentialPoints: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago
Over the next billion years plants evolved, gradually increasing atmospheric oxygen enabling animal evolution

nodes.label: Fuels contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may contain sulfur
nodes.objective: State that most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur as an impurity.
essentialPoints: Fuels such as coal contain carbon and/or hydrogen
Some fuels also contain sulfur impurities

nodes.label: Using appropriate significant figures
nodes.objective: Express calculated answers to an appropriate number of significant figures.
essentialPoints: Round answers to match precision of data given
Avoid over- or under-stating precision

nodes.label: Using ratios, fractions and percentages
nodes.objective: Apply ratio, fraction and percentage calculations to scientific data.
essentialPoints: Convert between ratio, fraction and percentage forms
Apply to compositions and comparisons

nodes.label: Translating information between graphical and numeric form
nodes.objective: Move between tables, charts, graphs and numerical data.
essentialPoints: Read values from charts/graphs/tables
Convert extracted data into calculations

nodes.label: Using orders of magnitude to evaluate data significance
nodes.objective: Compare quantities using orders of magnitude to judge significance.
essentialPoints: Estimate scale differences between large numbers
Judge whether a difference is meaningful

nodes.label: Titration technique using a burette and pipette
nodes.objective: Carry out an acid-alkali titration accurately using appropriate apparatus and an indicator to find the end point.
essentialPoints: Use pipette to measure fixed volume of one solution into a flask
Add indicator and run second solution from burette until colour change (end point)
Repeat to obtain concordant titre results

nodes.label: Concentration in mol/dm3 and converting to g/dm3
nodes.objective: Calculate and convert concentration between mol/dm3 and g/dm3.
essentialPoints: Concentration = moles / volume in dm3
Convert moles to mass using molar mass to get g/dm3

nodes.label: Measuring pH using indicators and probes
nodes.objective: Measure the pH of a solution using indicator paper/solution or a pH probe.
essentialPoints: pH scale indicates acidity/alkalinity
Indicators or electronic probes give a pH reading

nodes.label: Evaporation and crystallisation technique
nodes.objective: Obtain solid crystals from a solution by evaporating solvent and cooling to crystallise.
essentialPoints: Heat solution to evaporate solvent until saturated
Cool to allow crystals to form and filter/dry them

nodes.label: Simple distillation technique
nodes.objective: Separate a liquid from a solution/mixture using simple distillation apparatus.
essentialPoints: Heat mixture, vapour rises and passes through condenser
Condensed liquid (distillate) collected separately from residue

nodes.label: Dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle
nodes.objective: Explain how reversible reactions reach dynamic equilibrium and how conditions shift the position of equilibrium.
essentialPoints: In a closed system reversible reaction reaches equilibrium when forward and reverse rates are equal
Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant but reactions continue
Changing temperature, pressure or concentration shifts equilibrium position (Le Chatelier)

nodes.label: Factors affecting rate of reaction (temperature, concentration, pressure, catalysts)
nodes.objective: Explain how temperature, concentration, pressure and catalysts affect reaction rate via collision theory.
essentialPoints: Higher temperature/concentration/pressure increases collision frequency and rate
Catalysts provide a lower activation energy pathway without being used up

nodes.label: Reactivity series of metals
nodes.objective: Recall the relative reactivity of common metals and use it to predict displacement reactions.
essentialPoints: Metals can be ranked by reactivity
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound

nodes.label: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions
nodes.objective: Explain the products formed at electrodes during electrolysis of aqueous solutions.
essentialPoints: Cations move to cathode, anions to anode
At the cathode: hydrogen unless a less reactive metal ion present
At the anode: oxygen unless halide ions present (then halogen)

nodes.label: Human use of Earth's resources for warmth, shelter, food and transport
nodes.objective: State how humans use Earth's resources to meet basic needs.
essentialPoints: Resources provide warmth, shelter, food and transport

nodes.label: Definition of potable water vs pure water
nodes.objective: Distinguish between potable water and chemically pure water.
essentialPoints: Potable water is safe to drink with low levels of dissolved salts and microbes
Potable water is not pure in the chemical sense as it contains dissolved substances

nodes.label: Polymer properties depend on monomer and production conditions
nodes.objective: Explain that polymer properties depend on the monomers used and the conditions of production.
essentialPoints: Different monomers and reaction conditions give polymers with different properties

nodes.label: Using scientific models to explain, predict and show limitations
nodes.objective: Use representational, spatial, descriptive and mathematical models to explain phenomena, make predictions and recognise their limitations.
essentialPoints: Models (diagrams, equations, representations) simplify real phenomena
Models can be used to make predictions or calculate quantities
Models have limitations and can be tested against experimental observation

nodes.label: Forming a hypothesis from scientific theory
nodes.objective: Suggest a testable hypothesis to explain given observations or data using scientific theory.
essentialPoints: A hypothesis is a testable explanation based on existing scientific theory
Hypotheses are proposed to explain observations before testing

nodes.label: Scientific quantities and how they are determined
nodes.objective: Recognise the importance of scientific quantities and understand how they are determined experimentally.
essentialPoints: A scientific quantity has both a numerical value and a unit
Quantities are determined through defined measurement procedures

nodes.label: Standard and decimal form for numbers
nodes.objective: Recognise and use expressions in decimal and standard form.
essentialPoints: Numbers can be expressed in decimal form
Numbers can be expressed in standard form (a x 10^n)
Standard form is used for very large or very small numbers such as the Avogadro constant

nodes.label: Estimating the results of calculations
nodes.objective: Make estimates of the results of simple calculations to check plausibility of an answer.
essentialPoints: An estimate uses rounded values to quickly approximate a calculation result
Estimation is used to check whether a calculated answer is reasonable

nodes.label: Changing the subject of an equation
nodes.objective: Rearrange an algebraic equation to make a different quantity the subject.
essentialPoints: Rearranging isolates the required unknown quantity on one side of the equation
The same operation must be applied to both sides to preserve equality

nodes.label: Plotting two variables from experimental data
nodes.objective: Plot two variables from experimental or other data onto a graph with appropriate axes and scales.
essentialPoints: Independent variable is plotted on the x-axis, dependent on the y-axis
Axes must be scaled and labelled appropriately with units

nodes.label: Calculating areas and volumes of simple shapes
nodes.objective: Calculate areas of triangles and rectangles, and surface areas and volumes of cubes.
essentialPoints: Area of a rectangle = length × width; area of a triangle = 0.5 × base × height
Volume of a cube = side length cubed; surface area = 6 × side length squared

nodes.label: Element names and chemical symbols (first 20 elements, Groups 1 & 7, and others in spec)
nodes.objective: Recall and use the names and symbols of the first 20 elements, Group 1 and Group 7 elements, and other specified elements.
essentialPoints: Each element has a unique one- or two-letter chemical symbol (e.g. O, Na)
The first 20 elements plus Groups 1 and 7 and other spec elements must be known by name and symbol

nodes.label: Atomic model history: solid sphere and plum pudding models
nodes.objective: Describe the early solid sphere model of the atom and the plum pudding model that followed the discovery of the electron.
essentialPoints: Before the electron was discovered, atoms were thought to be tiny indivisible spheres
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model: a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it

nodes.label: Three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent, metallic
nodes.objective: State the three types of strong chemical bonding and the particles/forces involved in each.
essentialPoints: Ionic bonding: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
Covalent bonding: atoms sharing pairs of electrons
Metallic bonding: atoms sharing delocalised electrons
Bonding explained via electrostatic forces and electron transfer/sharing

nodes.label: Naming changes of state: melting, freezing, boiling, condensing at melting/boiling point
nodes.objective: Name the changes of state and state that they occur at the melting point or boiling point.
essentialPoints: Melting and freezing occur at the melting point
Boiling and condensing occur at the boiling point

nodes.label: Atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of the material
nodes.objective: Recognise that individual atoms do not display the bulk (macroscopic) properties of the material they form.
essentialPoints: A single atom cannot be described as having melting point, hardness etc.
Bulk properties arise from the collective structure and bonding of many atoms

nodes.label: State symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) in chemical equations
nodes.objective: Use the correct state symbols in chemical equations to represent solids, liquids, gases and aqueous solutions.
essentialPoints: (s) = solid, (l) = liquid, (g) = gas, (aq) = aqueous solution

nodes.label: Comparing nanoparticle dimensions to typical atom/molecule dimensions
nodes.objective: Compare nanoparticle dimensions to the typical dimensions of atoms and molecules using estimation and order-of-magnitude reasoning.
essentialPoints: Nanoparticles are of the order of a few hundred atoms across
Atoms/molecules are roughly 0.1-0.5 nm, much smaller than a nanoparticle

nodes.label: Balanced symbol equations and use of multipliers
nodes.objective: Balance symbol equations using multipliers before formulae and subscripts within formulae so atom numbers match on both sides.
essentialPoints: A balanced equation has equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides
Multipliers in normal script go before a formula and apply to the whole formula
Subscripts within a formula show fixed atom ratios within that substance

nodes.label: Reasons actual yield is less than theoretical yield
nodes.objective: Explain why the yield of a reaction is often less than the maximum theoretical amount even though mass is conserved.
essentialPoints: The reaction may be reversible and not go to completion
Product may be lost during separation from the reaction mixture
Some reactants may undergo unexpected/side reactions

nodes.label: Reactivity relates to a metal's tendency to form positive ions
nodes.objective: Explain that reactivity of a metal is related to how readily it loses electrons to form positive ions.
essentialPoints: More reactive metals lose electrons more readily
This tendency to form positive ions determines position in the series

nodes.label: Acids produce hydrogen ions (H+) in aqueous solution
nodes.objective: State that aqueous acids release hydrogen ions.
essentialPoints: Acids dissociate in water releasing H+ ions

nodes.label: Alkalis produce hydroxide ions (OH-) in aqueous solution
nodes.objective: State that aqueous alkalis release hydroxide ions.
essentialPoints: Alkalis dissociate in water releasing OH- ions

nodes.label: Electrolytes: molten/dissolved ionic compounds conduct via free-moving ions
nodes.objective: State that molten or dissolved ionic compounds are electrolytes because their ions are free to move and conduct electricity.
essentialPoints: Ions must be free to move (molten or in solution) to conduct
Solid ionic compounds do not conduct as ions are fixed in place

nodes.label: Neutralisation of acids by alkalis, bases and carbonates
nodes.objective: State that acids are neutralised by alkalis/bases to give salt and water, and by carbonates to give salt, water and carbon dioxide.
essentialPoints: Acid + alkali/base -> salt + water
Acid + carbonate -> salt + water + carbon dioxide

nodes.label: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides
nodes.objective: State that metals react with oxygen to produce metal oxides, an oxidation reaction.
essentialPoints: Metal + oxygen -> metal oxide
This is an oxidation reaction as the metal gains oxygen

nodes.label: Molar mass and moles = mass/Mr
nodes.objective: Convert between mass, moles and molar mass.
essentialPoints: moles = mass / molar mass
Molar mass from relative atomic/formula mass

nodes.label: Activation energy: the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur
nodes.objective: Define activation energy as the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.
essentialPoints: Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for particles to react on collision
Collisions with less than this energy do not result in a reaction

nodes.label: Exothermic reactions: definition
nodes.objective: Define an exothermic reaction as one that transfers energy to the surroundings, raising their temperature.
essentialPoints: Energy transferred to surroundings
Temperature of surroundings increases
Products have less energy than reactants, by the amount transferred

nodes.label: Endothermic reactions: definition
nodes.objective: Define an endothermic reaction as one that takes in energy from the surroundings, lowering their temperature.
essentialPoints: Energy taken in from surroundings
Temperature of surroundings decreases
Products have more energy than reactants, by the amount absorbed

nodes.label: Calculating overall energy change from bond energies (HT)
nodes.objective: Calculate the overall energy change of a reaction using given bond energies for bonds broken and bonds formed.
essentialPoints: Overall energy change = total energy to break bonds in reactants minus total energy released forming bonds in products
Sum bond energies for all bonds broken and all bonds formed using given values
A negative result indicates an exothermic reaction; a positive result indicates endothermic

nodes.label: Factors affecting the voltage produced by a cell
nodes.objective: State that cell voltage depends on the type of electrode and the type of electrolyte used.
essentialPoints: Choice of metal electrodes affects the voltage produced
Choice of electrolyte affects the voltage produced

nodes.label: Battery: two or more cells connected in series
nodes.objective: Define a battery as two or more cells connected together in series to provide a greater voltage than a single cell.
essentialPoints: A battery is made of two or more cells connected in series
Connecting cells in series increases the total voltage produced

nodes.label: Mean rate of reaction formula (quantity of reactant used or product formed / time)
nodes.objective: Calculate the mean rate of a reaction from the quantity of reactant used or product formed and the time taken.
essentialPoints: mean rate = quantity of reactant used / time taken
mean rate = quantity of product formed / time taken
Quantity may be measured as mass (g) or volume (cm3), giving units g/s or cm3/s

nodes.label: Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates equal in a closed system
nodes.objective: Define equilibrium in a reversible reaction as the state reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
essentialPoints: Equilibrium requires a closed system that prevents escape of reactants and products
At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions still occur but at exactly the same rate
The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but not necessarily equal) at equilibrium

nodes.label: Energy changes in reversible reactions: exothermic one way, endothermic the other, equal magnitude
nodes.objective: Explain that if a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction it is endothermic in the reverse direction, with the same quantity of energy transferred each way.
essentialPoints: If the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic, and vice versa
The magnitude of energy transferred is the same in both directions

nodes.label: Crude oil: origin, finite resource, mixture of hydrocarbons
nodes.objective: Describe crude oil as a finite fossil resource formed from ancient biomass and consisting mainly of hydrocarbons.
essentialPoints: Crude oil is a finite resource found in rocks
It formed from the remains of ancient biomass (mainly plankton) buried in mud
Crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds, mostly hydrocarbons

nodes.label: Rf value: definition and calculation (distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent)
nodes.objective: Calculate the Rf value of a spot on a chromatogram using the formula.
essentialPoints: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent
Rf values are unitless ratios always between 0 and 1

nodes.label: Flame test procedure (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Carry out a flame test safely to observe the colour produced by a metal ion sample in a flame.
essentialPoints: A clean wire loop is dipped in the sample and held in a blue Bunsen flame
The resulting flame colour is observed and recorded

nodes.label: Test for hydrogen gas (lit splint 'pop' test)
nodes.objective: Describe and carry out the test for hydrogen gas using a lit splint.
essentialPoints: A burning splint held at the mouth of a test tube of gas produces a squeaky 'pop' if hydrogen is present

nodes.label: Test for oxygen gas (glowing splint relights)
nodes.objective: Describe and carry out the test for oxygen gas using a glowing splint.
essentialPoints: A glowing splint inserted into a test tube of gas relights if oxygen is present

nodes.label: Test for carbon dioxide gas (limewater turns milky)
nodes.objective: Describe and carry out the test for carbon dioxide gas using limewater.
essentialPoints: Limewater (aqueous calcium hydroxide) turns cloudy/milky when carbon dioxide is bubbled through or shaken with it

nodes.label: Test for chlorine gas (bleaches damp litmus paper)
nodes.objective: Describe and carry out the test for chlorine gas using damp litmus paper.
essentialPoints: Damp litmus paper is bleached and turns white in the presence of chlorine gas

nodes.label: Using melting point and boiling point data to distinguish pure substances from mixtures
nodes.objective: Use melting/boiling point data to determine whether a sample is pure or a mixture.
essentialPoints: Pure elements and compounds melt/boil at one specific, sharp temperature
Mixtures melt/boil over a range of temperatures, often below the pure melting point

nodes.label: Formulations: mixtures designed as useful products with measured components
nodes.objective: Define a formulation and identify examples/formulations given appropriate information.
essentialPoints: A formulation is a mixture designed to have specific useful properties
Components are mixed in carefully measured quantities
Examples include fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers, foods

nodes.label: Practical procedure for paper chromatography of coloured substances
nodes.objective: Set up and run a paper chromatogram, applying spots correctly and running solvent up the paper without submerging the spots.
essentialPoints: A baseline is drawn in pencil and spots of sample applied above the solvent level
The paper is placed in solvent with the baseline above the solvent surface
The chromatogram is removed once the solvent front has risen sufficiently and left to dry

nodes.label: Identity and colour of metal hydroxide precipitates (Al, Ca, Mg, Cu, Fe(II), Fe(III)) (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Recall the precipitate colour produced by each named metal ion with sodium hydroxide solution.
essentialPoints: Aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions form white precipitates
Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate, iron(II) a green precipitate, iron(III) a brown precipitate

nodes.label: Precipitate colours for chloride, bromide and iodide with silver nitrate (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Recall the colour of the silver halide precipitate formed for each named halide ion.
essentialPoints: Silver chloride is white
Silver bromide is cream
Silver iodide is yellow

nodes.label: White precipitate (barium sulfate) as positive result for sulfate ions (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: State that a white precipitate of barium sulfate confirms the presence of sulfate ions.
essentialPoints: A white precipitate forms with barium chloride solution if sulfate ions are present

nodes.label: Dissolving of CO2 in oceans and formation of carbonate sediments
nodes.objective: Explain how CO2 dissolved in forming oceans and was precipitated as carbonates, reducing atmospheric CO2.
essentialPoints: When oceans formed, CO2 dissolved into the water
Carbonates precipitated out of solution forming sedimentary rock deposits
This process reduced the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere

nodes.label: Photosynthesis as a cause of decreasing atmospheric CO2
nodes.objective: Explain how photosynthesis by algae and plants decreased the percentage of CO2 in the atmosphere.
essentialPoints: Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the atmosphere and locks carbon into biomass
Contributed to long-term decline in atmospheric CO2 percentage

nodes.label: Greenhouse gases: water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane
nodes.objective: Identify water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane as the main greenhouse gases responsible for maintaining habitable temperatures on Earth.
essentialPoints: Greenhouse gases include water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane
They maintain Earth's temperature at a level able to support life

nodes.label: Purpose and raw materials of the Haber process
nodes.objective: State the purpose of the Haber process and recall the sources of nitrogen and hydrogen.
essentialPoints: Haber process manufactures ammonia for nitrogen-based fertilisers
Nitrogen obtained from the air; hydrogen obtained from natural gas (or other sources)

nodes.label: Natural resources supplemented/replaced by agricultural and synthetic products
nodes.objective: Give examples of natural products supplemented or replaced by agricultural and synthetic products.
essentialPoints: Natural resources plus agriculture provide food, timber, clothing, fuel
Synthetic/agricultural products can supplement or replace natural ones (e.g. synthetic fibres replacing wool/cotton)

nodes.label: Interpreting resource data from charts, graphs and tables
nodes.objective: Extract and interpret information about resources from charts, graphs and tables, using orders of magnitude to judge significance.
essentialPoints: Read resource-use data from given charts/graphs/tables
Use orders of magnitude to evaluate whether differences are significant

nodes.label: Producing potable water from fresh water (UK method)
nodes.objective: Describe the steps used to produce potable water from fresh water sources in the UK.
essentialPoints: Choose an appropriate fresh water source
Pass water through filter beds to remove solids
Sterilise using chlorine, ozone or UV light

nodes.label: Desalination methods for salty/sea water
nodes.objective: Describe desalination by distillation or reverse osmosis when fresh water supplies are limited.
essentialPoints: Distillation evaporates and condenses water to remove dissolved salts
Reverse osmosis uses membranes to filter out salts
Both processes require large amounts of energy

nodes.label: Required practical 8: analysis and purification of water samples
nodes.objective: Analyse and purify water samples from different sources, measuring pH and dissolved solids and using distillation.
essentialPoints: Measure pH of water samples using indicator/probe
Evaporate a known volume to find mass of dissolved solids
Distil a sample to obtain purified water and compare with original

nodes.label: Need for waste water treatment
nodes.objective: Explain why sewage, agricultural and industrial waste water need treatment before release.
essentialPoints: Sewage/agricultural waste water contains organic matter and harmful microbes
Industrial waste water may contain organic matter and harmful chemicals

nodes.label: LD and HD poly(ethene) from ethene
nodes.objective: Explain how low density and high density poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene under different conditions.
essentialPoints: Both LD and HD poly(ethene) are made by polymerising the same monomer, ethene
Different reaction conditions (temperature, pressure, catalyst) give the two different forms

nodes.label: Thermosoftening vs thermosetting polymers
nodes.objective: Explain the difference between thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers in terms of their structures.
essentialPoints: Thermosoftening polymers have individual tangled chains with weak intermolecular forces, so melt on heating
Thermosetting polymers have cross-links between chains, so do not melt when heated

nodes.label: Power and limitations of science; ethical issues
nodes.objective: Explain why scientific data may be uncertain or incomplete, and outline ethical arguments about new technologies.
essentialPoints: Data is needed to answer scientific questions but may be incomplete or uncertain
Science cannot answer questions of ethics, only inform them
Ethical arguments weigh rights and wrongs of new technology

nodes.label: Planning experimental procedures
nodes.objective: Plan or devise an experimental procedure to test a hypothesis, make observations, or characterise a substance, controlling relevant variables.
essentialPoints: A well-designed procedure controls variables to allow valid conclusions
Procedures must be suited to their specific purpose (observation, testing, characterisation)

nodes.label: Using SI units and chemical nomenclature
nodes.objective: Use SI units (e.g. kg, g, mg, km, m, mm, kJ, J) and IUPAC chemical nomenclature correctly.
essentialPoints: SI units are the standard units used to express physical quantities in science
IUPAC nomenclature provides standardised chemical naming

nodes.label: Using an appropriate number of significant figures
nodes.objective: Round and report calculated answers to an appropriate number of significant figures.
essentialPoints: A calculated answer should not be given to more significant figures than the least precise data used
Rounding rules for significant figures

nodes.label: Translating data between graphical and numeric forms
nodes.objective: Convert data between tabular/numeric form and graphical representation.
essentialPoints: Data presented as a table can be represented as a graph and vice versa
Choosing the correct representation depends on the type of data (continuous/discrete)

nodes.label: Determining slope and intercept of a linear graph
nodes.objective: Determine the gradient and y-intercept of a straight-line graph and relate this to y = mx + c.
essentialPoints: The gradient is calculated as change in y divided by change in x
The y-intercept is the value of y where the line crosses the y-axis
A straight-line graph follows the form y = mx + c

nodes.label: Finding area between a curve and the x-axis
nodes.objective: Understand the physical significance of the area between a curve and the x-axis and measure it by counting squares.
essentialPoints: The area under a graph can represent a physically meaningful quantity
This area can be estimated by counting the squares beneath the curve

nodes.label: Compounds and chemical reactions
nodes.objective: Define compounds and describe how chemical reactions form new substances.
essentialPoints: Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions
Chemical reactions always form one or more new substances, often with a detectable energy change
Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions
Compounds are represented by formulae using element symbols

nodes.label: How new evidence changes a scientific model
nodes.objective: Explain that scientific models are changed or replaced when new experimental evidence emerges.
essentialPoints: A scientific model can be changed or replaced when new evidence does not fit the existing model
This is illustrated by the historical development of the atomic model

nodes.label: Which substances show which bond type (metal+nonmetal, nonmetal elements/compounds, metals/alloys)
nodes.objective: Identify which type of bonding occurs in a given substance based on its composition.
essentialPoints: Ionic bonding occurs in compounds of metals with non-metals
Covalent bonding occurs in non-metallic elements and compounds of non-metals
Metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys

nodes.label: Energy needed for state change depends on strength of forces between particles (bonding/structure)
nodes.objective: Explain that the energy required to change state depends on the strength of the forces between particles, which depends on bonding type and structure.
essentialPoints: Stronger forces between particles require more energy to change state
Nature of particles/forces depends on the type of bonding and structure
Stronger forces mean higher melting and boiling points

nodes.label: Nanoparticles have different properties from bulk material due to high surface area to volume ratio
nodes.objective: Explain that nanoparticles may have different properties from the same material in bulk because of their high surface area to volume ratio, and that smaller quantities may be needed to be effective.
essentialPoints: High surface area to volume ratio changes reactivity/behaviour compared to bulk
Smaller quantities of nanoparticulate material may be needed to be as effective as bulk material

nodes.label: Relative formula mass (Mr)
nodes.objective: Calculate the relative formula mass of a compound as the sum of relative atomic masses of its atoms.
essentialPoints: Mr is the sum of relative atomic masses of all atoms shown in the formula
Uses relative atomic masses (Ar) from the periodic table

nodes.label: Mass changes in non-enclosed systems involving gases
nodes.objective: Explain apparent changes in mass in open reactions where a reactant or product is a gas, using the particle model and a balanced equation.
essentialPoints: Mass appears to increase when a gas reactant (e.g. oxygen) is taken in from the surroundings and becomes part of a solid product
Mass appears to decrease when a gas product (e.g. CO2 from thermal decomposition) escapes into the atmosphere
Total mass is conserved when the escaped/absorbed gas is accounted for

nodes.label: Calculating percentage yield
nodes.objective: Calculate the percentage yield of a product from the actual mass obtained and the maximum theoretical mass.
essentialPoints: % yield = (mass of product actually made / maximum theoretical mass) x 100

nodes.label: The reactivity series of metals (K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu + H, C)
nodes.objective: Recall the order of reactivity of named metals plus carbon and hydrogen.
essentialPoints: Order: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper
Carbon and hydrogen are often included as reference points

nodes.label: Strong and weak acids in terms of degree of ionisation (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain the difference between strong and weak acids in terms of degree of ionisation.
essentialPoints: Strong acids fully ionise in water (HCl, HNO3, H2SO4)
Weak acids only partially ionise (ethanoic, citric, carbonic acids)

nodes.label: The pH scale (0-14) and its meaning
nodes.objective: State that pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline.
essentialPoints: pH scale runs 0 to 14
pH<7 acidic, pH=7 neutral, pH>7 alkaline

nodes.label: The process of electrolysis: ion movement and discharge at electrodes
nodes.objective: Describe how passing a current through an electrolyte causes ions to move to and be discharged at electrodes.
essentialPoints: Positive ions move to the negative electrode (cathode)
Negative ions move to the positive electrode (anode) and are discharged as elements

nodes.label: Water molecules break down to give H+ and OH- ions in aqueous electrolysis
nodes.objective: Explain that water breaks down to produce H+ and OH- ions which can be discharged at electrodes.
essentialPoints: Water partially ionises into H+ and OH- ions
These ions can be discharged instead of the dissolved compound's ions

nodes.label: Which acid produces which salt type (chloride, nitrate, sulfate)
nodes.objective: State that hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, nitric acid gives nitrates, sulfuric acid gives sulfates.
essentialPoints: Hydrochloric acid -> chloride salts
Nitric acid -> nitrate salts; sulfuric acid -> sulfate salts

nodes.label: Method for making a soluble salt from an insoluble solid and acid
nodes.objective: Describe how to prepare a pure, dry soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble metal/oxide/hydroxide/carbonate.
essentialPoints: Add excess insoluble solid to acid until no more reacts
Filter off excess solid, then evaporate/crystallise filtrate to obtain dry salt crystals

nodes.label: Neutralisation ionic equation: H+ + OH- -> H2O
nodes.objective: State the ionic equation representing neutralisation between an acid and alkali.
essentialPoints: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)
Represents the common reaction in all acid-alkali neutralisations

nodes.label: Oxidation and reduction defined by loss/gain of oxygen
nodes.objective: Explain oxidation and reduction in terms of gain or loss of oxygen.
essentialPoints: Oxidation = gain of oxygen
Reduction = loss of oxygen

nodes.label: Collision theory: reactions require collisions with sufficient energy
nodes.objective: Explain that reactions occur only when particles collide with each other with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.
essentialPoints: Reacting particles must collide for a reaction to happen
Collisions must have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy to be successful
Rate depends on both frequency of collisions and their energy

nodes.label: Examples of exothermic reactions: combustion, oxidation, neutralisation
nodes.objective: Recall named reaction types that are exothermic.
essentialPoints: Combustion reactions are exothermic
Many oxidation reactions are exothermic
Neutralisation reactions are exothermic

nodes.label: Fuel cells: definition
nodes.objective: Describe a fuel cell as a cell supplied with an external fuel and oxygen/air, in which the fuel is oxidised electrochemically to produce a potential difference.
essentialPoints: Fuel cell is supplied continuously from an external source of fuel and oxygen or air
Fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the cell
This produces a potential difference (voltage)

nodes.label: Examples of endothermic reactions: thermal decomposition, citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate
nodes.objective: Recall named reaction types that are endothermic.
essentialPoints: Thermal decomposition reactions are endothermic
Reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate is endothermic

nodes.label: Distinguishing exothermic and endothermic reactions from temperature change
nodes.objective: Classify a reaction as exothermic or endothermic based on observed change in surroundings temperature.
essentialPoints: Rise in surroundings temperature indicates an exothermic reaction
Fall in surroundings temperature indicates an endothermic reaction

nodes.label: Drawing reaction profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions
nodes.objective: Draw a reaction profile with a curved line showing reactant energy, product energy, activation energy and overall energy change.
essentialPoints: Curved line shows energy of the system as the reaction proceeds
Products drawn lower than reactants for exothermic, higher for endothermic
Activation energy shown as the peak above the reactant energy level

nodes.label: Explaining exothermic reactions using bond energies (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain that a reaction is exothermic when more energy is released forming bonds than is used breaking bonds.
essentialPoints: Energy released forming new bonds is greater than energy needed to break existing bonds
Net energy is transferred to the surroundings

nodes.label: Explaining endothermic reactions using bond energies (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain that a reaction is endothermic when more energy is used breaking bonds than is released forming bonds.
essentialPoints: Energy needed to break existing bonds is greater than energy released forming new bonds
Net energy is absorbed from the surroundings

nodes.label: Interpreting relative reactivity data of metals for cell voltage
nodes.objective: Use given reactivity data for different metals to interpret or predict relative voltages produced by simple cells.
essentialPoints: Greater difference in reactivity between the two metals generally produces a greater voltage
Use given data (e.g. voltage tables) to rank or compare metal combinations

nodes.label: Non-rechargeable cells and batteries
nodes.objective: Define non-rechargeable cells/batteries as those where the chemical reaction stops once a reactant is used up.
essentialPoints: Chemical reaction stops when one reactant is fully used up
Cannot be reversed by supplying electrical current
Alkaline batteries are an example

nodes.label: Rechargeable cells and batteries
nodes.objective: Define rechargeable cells/batteries as those in which the chemical reaction can be reversed by an external electrical current.
essentialPoints: Chemical reactions in the cell can be reversed when an external current is supplied
This restores the original reactants, allowing repeated use

nodes.label: Rate of reaction in moles and mol/s (HT only)
nodes.objective: Express quantity of reactant or product in moles and calculate rate in mol/s.
essentialPoints: Quantity of substance can be expressed in moles instead of mass or volume
Rate can then be given in mol/s

nodes.label: Drawing and interpreting graphs of quantity vs time for reactions
nodes.objective: Draw and interpret graphs showing quantity of product formed or reactant used against time, recognising how curve steepness relates to rate.
essentialPoints: A steeper slope means a faster rate of reaction at that point
The curve levels off (plateaus) when the reaction has finished
Different conditions produce different curve shapes on the same axes

nodes.label: Concentration as a factor affecting rate of reaction
nodes.objective: Recall that concentration of reactants in solution affects rate of reaction.
essentialPoints: Concentration of reactants in solution is a factor that affects rate of reaction

nodes.label: Pressure as a factor affecting rate of reaction
nodes.objective: Recall that pressure of reacting gases affects rate of reaction.
essentialPoints: Pressure of reacting gases is a factor that affects rate of reaction

nodes.label: Surface area as a factor affecting rate of reaction
nodes.objective: Recall that surface area of solid reactants affects rate of reaction.
essentialPoints: Surface area of solid reactants is a factor that affects rate of reaction

nodes.label: Temperature as a factor affecting rate of reaction
nodes.objective: Recall that temperature affects rate of reaction.
essentialPoints: Temperature is a factor that affects rate of reaction

nodes.label: Presence of a catalyst as a factor affecting rate of reaction
nodes.objective: Recall that the presence of a catalyst affects rate of reaction.
essentialPoints: Presence of a catalyst is a factor that affects rate of reaction

nodes.label: Le Chatelier's Principle (HT only)
nodes.objective: State Le Chatelier's Principle: if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the system responds to counteract that change.
essentialPoints: If conditions of a system at equilibrium are changed, the position of equilibrium shifts to counteract the change
This allows qualitative prediction of the effect of changes in concentration, temperature or pressure on equilibrium position

nodes.label: Hydrocarbons: molecules of hydrogen and carbon only
nodes.objective: Define a hydrocarbon as a molecule containing only hydrogen and carbon atoms.
essentialPoints: A hydrocarbon contains only hydrogen and carbon atoms

nodes.label: Flame test colours for lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper ions (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Recall the characteristic flame colour produced by each of five named metal ions.
essentialPoints: Lithium = crimson, sodium = yellow, potassium = lilac
Calcium = orange-red, copper = green

nodes.label: Test for carbonate ions using dilute acid and limewater (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Test for carbonate ions by reacting with dilute acid and identifying the carbon dioxide gas produced using limewater.
essentialPoints: Carbonates react with dilute acids to produce carbon dioxide gas
The gas produced is confirmed as carbon dioxide using the limewater test

nodes.label: Using chromatography to distinguish pure from impure substances
nodes.objective: Explain how the number of spots on a chromatogram indicates whether a substance is pure or a mixture.
essentialPoints: A pure compound produces a single spot in any solvent
A mixture may separate into multiple spots
The same substance run in different solvents can be checked for consistency of a single spot across solvents

nodes.label: Identifying formulations from given information
nodes.objective: Given a description of a mixture and its components' purposes, identify it as a formulation.
essentialPoints: Recognise a mixture as a formulation when its components each serve a specific measured purpose

nodes.label: Interpreting chromatograms and determining Rf values from experimental data
nodes.objective: Measure distances on a chromatogram and calculate Rf values from the results to identify substances.
essentialPoints: Measure distance from baseline to centre of spot and to solvent front
Different compounds have different, characteristic Rf values in a given solvent
Comparing Rf values to known references can identify unknown compounds

nodes.label: Aluminium hydroxide dissolving in excess sodium hydroxide, distinguishing it from calcium/magnesium (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Explain that only aluminium hydroxide, among the white precipitates, redissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution, distinguishing aluminium ions from calcium and magnesium ions.
essentialPoints: Aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess NaOH solution, but calcium hydroxide and magnesium hydroxide do not
This allows aluminium ions to be distinguished from calcium/magnesium ions despite all forming white precipitates initially

nodes.label: Balanced equations for formation of insoluble metal hydroxide precipitates (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Write balanced equations (including ionic equations) for the reaction of metal ions with hydroxide ions to form insoluble metal hydroxides.
essentialPoints: Metal ion + hydroxide ion → insoluble metal hydroxide precipitate
Equations must be balanced for atoms and charge
Equations for the formation of sodium aluminate are not required

nodes.label: Identifying an unknown halide ion from precipitate colour with silver nitrate (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Use the observed precipitate colour to identify which halide ion is present in a solution.
essentialPoints: Match the observed precipitate colour to the corresponding halide ion

nodes.label: Evaluating evidence and theories about Earth's early atmosphere
nodes.objective: Given appropriate information, interpret evidence and evaluate different theories about the composition and formation of Earth's early atmosphere.
essentialPoints: Evidence for the early atmosphere is limited due to the 4.6 billion year timescale
Different theories can be compared and evaluated against given evidence
Uncertainty exists because direct measurement of ancient atmospheres is impossible

nodes.label: Formation of limestone, coal, crude oil and natural gas as carbon sinks
nodes.objective: Describe and explain the formation of deposits of limestone, coal, crude oil and natural gas, and how their formation removed carbon from the atmosphere-ocean system.
essentialPoints: Sedimentary rocks such as limestone formed from precipitated carbonates and shells/skeletons of marine organisms
Coal formed from the remains of ancient plants under heat and pressure over geological time
Crude oil and natural gas formed from the remains of marine organisms buried under sediment over geological time
These deposits locked carbon away, reducing atmospheric/dissolved CO2

nodes.label: The greenhouse effect: interaction of short and long wavelength radiation with matter
nodes.objective: Describe the greenhouse effect in terms of short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passing through the atmosphere, being absorbed and re-emitted as longer-wavelength radiation, which greenhouse gases absorb and re-radiate, warming the Earth's surface.
essentialPoints: Short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the Earth's surface
The Earth re-emits energy as longer-wavelength radiation
Greenhouse gases absorb this long-wavelength radiation and re-radiate it in all directions, including back to Earth's surface
This traps energy in the lower atmosphere, raising surface temperature

nodes.label: Reversible reaction in the Haber process
nodes.objective: State the reversible reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen to form ammonia.
essentialPoints: Nitrogen and hydrogen react reversibly to form ammonia
Some ammonia produced breaks back down into nitrogen and hydrogen

nodes.label: NPK fertilisers improve agricultural productivity
nodes.objective: State that NPK fertilisers contain compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium to improve agricultural productivity.
essentialPoints: Compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are used as fertilisers
NPK fertilisers are formulations containing all three elements

nodes.label: Finite vs renewable resources
nodes.objective: Distinguish between finite and renewable resources given appropriate information.
essentialPoints: Finite resources are used up faster than they form (e.g. fossil fuels, metal ores)
Renewable resources are replenished at a usable rate (e.g. timber, wind)

nodes.label: Reasons for each step in potable water production
nodes.objective: Give reasons for the steps used to produce potable water.
essentialPoints: Filtration removes suspended solids and larger impurities
Sterilisation kills/removes harmful microbes
Source choice depends on availability of low-dissolved-substance fresh water

nodes.label: Comparing treatment of ground water vs salty/sea water
nodes.objective: Describe differences in treatment between ground water and salty water in producing potable water.
essentialPoints: Ground/fresh water needs only filtration and sterilisation
Salty/sea water needs energy-intensive desalination in addition

nodes.label: Calculating mass of dissolved solids from evaporation data
nodes.objective: Calculate the mass/concentration of dissolved solids in a water sample from evaporation results.
essentialPoints: Mass of residue after evaporation indicates dissolved solid content
Divide by volume of sample to find concentration of dissolved solids

nodes.label: Screening and grit removal
nodes.objective: Describe screening and grit removal as the first stage of sewage treatment.
essentialPoints: Removes large solid objects and grit from sewage

nodes.label: Comparing thermosetting and thermosoftening polymer properties
nodes.objective: Compare the properties of thermosetting and thermosoftening polymers.
essentialPoints: Thermosoftening polymers soften/melt and can be reshaped/recycled by heating
Thermosetting polymers remain rigid and do not melt, so are harder and more heat resistant

nodes.label: Evaluating applications and implications of science
nodes.objective: Describe and evaluate technological applications of science including personal, social, economic and environmental implications.
essentialPoints: Applications of science have personal, social, economic and environmental impacts
Decisions about science-based issues should be based on evaluation of evidence and arguments

nodes.label: Peer review and communicating scientific results
nodes.objective: Explain the purpose of peer review and why media reports of science may be unreliable.
essentialPoints: Peer review checks scientific claims before publication to detect false claims and build consensus
Media reports are not peer reviewed and may be oversimplified, inaccurate or biased

nodes.label: Selecting appropriate apparatus, techniques and materials
nodes.objective: Select and justify the technique, instrument, apparatus or material appropriate for a given experimental purpose.
essentialPoints: Different instruments/apparatus suit different purposes and required precision
Justification of choice depends on the specific experimental context

nodes.label: Sampling techniques to obtain representative samples
nodes.objective: Suggest and describe an appropriate sampling technique to ensure samples collected are representative.
essentialPoints: A representative sample reflects the properties of the whole population or material being tested
Sampling technique choice depends on the context and material

nodes.label: Using prefixes and powers of ten for orders of magnitude
nodes.objective: Use standard prefixes (tera, giga, mega, kilo, centi, milli, micro, nano) and powers of ten to express orders of magnitude.
essentialPoints: Prefixes represent specific powers of ten applied to a base unit
Powers of ten allow very large or very small quantities to be expressed concisely

nodes.label: Making order of magnitude calculations
nodes.objective: Make estimates of quantities to the correct order of magnitude, using powers of ten.
essentialPoints: An order of magnitude estimate expresses a quantity as a power of ten
Used to sanity-check whether a calculated answer is reasonable

nodes.label: Interpreting data: patterns, trends, inferences and conclusions
nodes.objective: Interpret data presented in verbal, diagrammatic, graphical, symbolic or numerical form to identify patterns, make inferences and draw conclusions.
essentialPoints: Patterns and trends in data can be identified across different presentation formats
Conclusions must be drawn directly from, and supported by, the data given
Data can be used to make predictions

nodes.label: Using the tangent to a curve to find rate of change
nodes.objective: Draw a tangent to a point on a curve and use its slope as a measure of the instantaneous rate of change.
essentialPoints: A tangent is a straight line touching a curve at a single point
The gradient of the tangent gives the instantaneous rate of change at that point

nodes.label: Writing word and balanced symbol equations
nodes.objective: Write word equations and balanced chemical equations (with state symbols/formulae) for reactions in the specification.
essentialPoints: Word equations show reactants and products by name
Balanced symbol equations use formulae with equal atoms of each element on both sides
Conservation of mass requires balancing

nodes.label: Mixtures
nodes.objective: Define a mixture and explain that no chemical reaction is needed to form or separate one.
essentialPoints: A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined
Each substance in a mixture keeps its own chemical properties
Mixtures can be separated by physical processes without new substances being made

nodes.label: Alpha particle scattering experiment and the nuclear model
nodes.objective: Explain how the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment led to replacement of the plum pudding model with the nuclear model.
essentialPoints: Alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil; most passed through but some deflected or bounced back
This showed mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus
This evidence replaced the plum pudding model with the nuclear model

nodes.label: Formation of ions by electron transfer (metal loses, non-metal gains)
nodes.objective: Explain how metal and non-metal atoms form ions by losing or gaining electrons.
essentialPoints: Metal atoms lose outer shell electrons to become positive ions
Non-metal atoms gain electrons to become negative ions
This occurs when a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom

nodes.label: Covalent bonding: atoms sharing pairs of electrons
nodes.objective: Define covalent bonding as atoms sharing pairs of electrons, forming strong bonds.
essentialPoints: Atoms share pairs of electrons
Covalent bonds between atoms are strong

nodes.label: Metallic bonding: giant structure with delocalised outer shell electrons
nodes.objective: Define metallic bonding as the sharing of delocalised outer shell electrons in a giant structure of metal atoms.
essentialPoints: Metals are giant structures of atoms in a regular pattern
Outer shell electrons become delocalised and free to move through the structure
Sharing of delocalised electrons gives strong metallic bonds

nodes.label: Predicting the state of a substance at a given temperature from melting/boiling point data
nodes.objective: Predict whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas at a given temperature using its melting and boiling points.
essentialPoints: Compare given temperature to melting point and boiling point
Below melting point = solid, between = liquid, above boiling point = gas

nodes.label: (HT) Limitations of the simple particle model (no forces, spheres, solid inelastic)
nodes.objective: Explain the limitations of the simple particle model in representing changes of state, given that it shows no forces and solid inelastic spheres.
essentialPoints: Model has no forces between particles, unlike reality
Particles shown as solid spheres, not representing internal structure
Spheres are shown as inelastic, unlike real atoms/molecules

nodes.label: Applications of nanoparticles (medicine, electronics, cosmetics/sun creams, deodorants, catalysts)
nodes.objective: Recall applications of nanoparticles in medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants, and as catalysts.
essentialPoints: Uses include medicine, electronics, cosmetics/sun creams, deodorants, catalysts
