nodes.label: Possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles
nodes.objective: Explain that there are possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles, such as unknown effects on health and the environment.
essentialPoints: Nanoparticles may be able to enter cells or the bloodstream due to their small size
Long-term health and environmental effects are not yet fully known
High surface area to volume ratio may increase toxicity or reactivity in the body

nodes.label: Sum of Mr of reactants equals sum of Mr of products in a balanced equation
nodes.objective: Show that in a balanced equation the sum of relative formula masses of reactants (in the quantities shown) equals that of the products.
essentialPoints: This follows from conservation of mass applied to a balanced equation
The quantities shown by the balancing numbers must be included in the sum

nodes.label: Percentage mass of an element in a compound
nodes.objective: Calculate the percentage by mass of an element in a compound given relative formula mass and relative atomic masses.
essentialPoints: % mass = (total mass of element in formula / Mr of compound) x 100

nodes.label: The mole and molar mass (HT)
nodes.objective: State that chemical amounts are measured in moles, and that the mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass.
essentialPoints: The mole (mol) is the unit for amount of substance
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams equals its Mr numerically
One mole of a substance contains the same number of particles as one mole of any other substance

nodes.label: Atom economy definition and importance
nodes.objective: State that atom economy measures the proportion of starting materials that end up as useful (desired) products, and why high atom economy matters.
essentialPoints: Atom economy is a measure of the mass of starting materials that end up as useful products
High atom economy reduces waste and is important for sustainable development and economic reasons

nodes.label: Reactions of named metals with water and dilute acids
nodes.objective: Describe and recall the reactions (if any) of potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron and copper with water or dilute acids.
essentialPoints: K, Na, Li react vigorously with cold water; Ca reacts moderately
Mg, Zn, Fe react slowly/not with cold water but react with dilute acids; Cu does not react with dilute acids

nodes.label: Displacement reactions: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one
nodes.objective: Predict and describe displacement reactions between a metal and a compound of a less reactive metal.
essentialPoints: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound
Used as evidence to build/confirm the reactivity series

nodes.label: Unreactive metals (e.g. gold) found native in the Earth
nodes.objective: State that very unreactive metals occur naturally as the metal itself.
essentialPoints: Gold is found uncombined because it is very unreactive
Most other metals occur as compounds requiring extraction

nodes.label: Dilute and concentrated in terms of amount of substance (HT)
nodes.objective: Distinguish dilute from concentrated in terms of amount of acid substance per volume, separate from strong/weak.
essentialPoints: Concentration describes amount of acid dissolved per volume, not degree of ionisation
A concentrated acid can be weak, and a dilute acid can be strong

nodes.label: Measuring pH using universal indicator or a pH probe
nodes.objective: Describe use of universal indicator or a pH probe to measure approximate pH.
essentialPoints: Universal indicator gives a colour matched to a pH chart
pH probe gives a direct numerical reading

nodes.label: Stronger acid at given concentration has lower pH (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain that for a given concentration, a stronger acid has a lower pH than a weaker acid.
essentialPoints: Greater degree of ionisation gives higher H+ concentration
Higher H+ concentration corresponds to lower pH

nodes.label: Electrolysis of molten binary ionic compounds
nodes.objective: Predict the products of electrolysing a molten binary ionic compound using inert electrodes.
essentialPoints: Metal forms at the cathode, non-metal at the anode
Example: molten lead bromide gives lead at cathode and bromine at anode

nodes.label: Cathode product rule for aqueous electrolysis (H2 unless metal less reactive than H)
nodes.objective: State that hydrogen is produced at the cathode unless the metal is less reactive than hydrogen.
essentialPoints: Hydrogen forms at the cathode if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen
If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen, the metal itself is deposited

nodes.label: Anode product rule for aqueous electrolysis (O2 unless halide present)
nodes.objective: State that oxygen is produced at the anode unless the solution contains halide ions, in which case the halogen is produced.
essentialPoints: Oxygen forms at the anode from aqueous solutions without halide ions
If halide ions are present, the halogen gas is produced instead

nodes.label: Predicting salt products from given acid and base/alkali/carbonate reactants
nodes.objective: Predict the products of a reaction between a given acid and base/alkali/carbonate.
essentialPoints: Combine identity of positive ion from base with acid's salt type
Include water (and CO2 if a carbonate) as co-products

nodes.label: Using formulae of common ions to deduce salt formulae
nodes.objective: Deduce the correct formula of a salt from the ionic charges of its constituent ions.
essentialPoints: Balance charges of metal ion and acid's anion
Write correct ratio of ions in the formula

nodes.label: Extraction of metals less reactive than carbon by reduction with carbon
nodes.objective: Explain that metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by reduction with carbon.
essentialPoints: Carbon displaces the metal from its oxide
This works only for metals below carbon in the reactivity series

nodes.label: Oxidation and reduction in terms of electron loss/gain (HT)
nodes.objective: Define oxidation as loss of electrons and reduction as gain of electrons.
essentialPoints: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons) - OIL
Reduction Is Gain (of electrons) - RIG

nodes.label: Everyday uses of exothermic reactions: self-heating cans, hand warmers
nodes.objective: Recall and evaluate applications of exothermic reactions in everyday products.
essentialPoints: Self-heating cans use an exothermic reaction to warm contents
Hand warmers use an exothermic reaction to release heat

nodes.label: Overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell
nodes.objective: State that the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell is the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water.
essentialPoints: Hydrogen is oxidised within the fuel cell
The product of the overall reaction is water
Oxygen is reduced in the process

nodes.label: Everyday uses of endothermic reactions: sports injury packs
nodes.objective: Recall and evaluate applications of endothermic reactions in everyday products.
essentialPoints: Instant cold packs for sports injuries use an endothermic reaction to absorb heat

nodes.label: Required practical 4: measuring temperature change in reacting solutions
nodes.objective: Carry out an investigation into variables affecting temperature change in reacting solutions (e.g. acid + metal, acid + carbonate, neutralisation, displacement).
essentialPoints: Measure mass/volume of reactants and initial and maximum/minimum temperature
Control variables such as concentration, volume and starting temperature to ensure a fair test
Repeat readings and calculate a mean to improve reliability

nodes.label: Reading reaction profiles to identify exothermic or endothermic reactions
nodes.objective: Use a given reaction profile diagram to determine whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic and to read off the activation energy and overall energy change.
essentialPoints: Products below reactants on the diagram indicates exothermic; products above indicates endothermic
Overall energy change is the vertical difference between reactant and product energy levels
Activation energy is the difference between reactant energy and the peak of the curve

nodes.label: Evaluating the use of cells and batteries
nodes.objective: Evaluate the suitability of rechargeable versus non-rechargeable cells and batteries for given applications.
essentialPoints: Rechargeable batteries reduce waste and long-term cost but may have lower voltage stability or higher upfront cost
Non-rechargeable batteries are simpler and cheaper initially but must be replaced and disposed of once used up
Suitability depends on context such as frequency of use, cost and environmental impact

nodes.label: Using tangents on quantity-time graphs to find rate at a specific time
nodes.objective: Draw a tangent to a quantity-time curve at a given point and use its gradient to determine the rate of reaction at that specific time.
essentialPoints: Draw a tangent at the point of interest on the curve
The gradient of the tangent equals the rate of reaction at that instant
(HT) calculate the numerical value of the gradient as the rate

nodes.label: Explaining the effect of concentration on rate using collision theory
nodes.objective: Use collision theory to explain why increasing concentration of reactants in solution increases the rate of reaction.
essentialPoints: Higher concentration means more particles in a given volume
This increases the frequency of collisions between reacting particles
More frequent successful collisions increases rate

nodes.label: Explaining the effect of pressure on rate using collision theory
nodes.objective: Use collision theory to explain why increasing the pressure of reacting gases increases the rate of reaction.
essentialPoints: Higher pressure squeezes the same number of gas particles into a smaller volume
This increases the frequency of collisions between reacting particles
More frequent successful collisions increases rate

nodes.label: Surface area to volume ratio of solid particles
nodes.objective: Explain that breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases its surface area to volume ratio.
essentialPoints: Smaller pieces of the same total mass have a greater total surface area exposed
Surface area to volume ratio increases as particle size decreases
This exposes more particles at the surface to potential collisions

nodes.label: Explaining the effect of temperature on rate using collision theory
nodes.objective: Use collision theory to explain why increasing temperature increases the rate of reaction via both frequency and energy of collisions.
essentialPoints: Higher temperature makes particles move faster, increasing collision frequency
Higher temperature also increases the energy of collisions, so a greater proportion of collisions exceed the activation energy
Both effects combine to increase rate more than concentration/pressure/surface area changes alone

nodes.label: Definition of a catalyst
nodes.objective: Define a catalyst as a substance that changes the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up or appearing in the chemical equation.
essentialPoints: A catalyst changes (usually increases) the rate of a reaction
A catalyst is not used up during the reaction and is not included in the chemical equation
Different reactions require different catalysts, and enzymes act as biological catalysts

nodes.label: Effect of concentration changes on equilibrium position (HT only)
nodes.objective: Predict how changing the concentration of a reactant or product shifts a system away from and back to equilibrium.
essentialPoints: Increasing the concentration of a reactant causes more products to form until equilibrium is re-established
Decreasing the concentration of a product causes more reactants to react until equilibrium is re-established
Changing concentration takes the system out of equilibrium until concentrations adjust to restore it

nodes.label: Effect of temperature changes on equilibrium position (HT only)
nodes.objective: Predict how changing temperature shifts the equilibrium position depending on whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
essentialPoints: Increasing temperature increases the relative amount of products for an endothermic (forward) reaction
Increasing temperature decreases the relative amount of products for an exothermic (forward) reaction
Decreasing temperature has the opposite effects in each case

nodes.label: Effect of pressure changes on equilibrium position for gaseous reactions (HT only)
nodes.objective: Predict how changing pressure shifts the equilibrium position for gaseous reactions based on the relative numbers of gas molecules on each side.
essentialPoints: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas molecules, as shown by the symbol equation
Decreasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with more gas molecules
Requires comparing the number of moles of gas shown on each side of the balanced symbol equation

nodes.label: Alkanes: general formula CnH2n+2 and first four members
nodes.objective: State the general formula for alkanes and name/recognise the first four members from formulae or diagrams.
essentialPoints: Alkanes are a homologous series with general formula CnH2n+2
The first four alkanes are methane, ethane, propane and butane
Alkanes can be represented as molecular formulae or displayed/skeletal structures

nodes.label: Masking of flame colours in mixtures of ions (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Explain that a mixture of ions can mask or obscure individual flame colours.
essentialPoints: When a sample contains a mixture of metal ions, some flame colours can be hidden by others (e.g. a strong sodium yellow can mask other colours)

nodes.label: Flame emission spectroscopy: method and line spectrum output (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Describe how flame emission spectroscopy analyses metal ions by passing light from a flamed sample through a spectroscope to produce a line spectrum.
essentialPoints: The sample is introduced into a flame and the light emitted is passed through a spectroscope
The output is a line spectrum characteristic of the metal ions present
The spectrum can identify the ions present and measure their concentration

nodes.label: Identifying an unknown metal ion from its reaction with sodium hydroxide solution (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Use observations of precipitate colour and behaviour in excess NaOH to identify an unknown metal ion.
essentialPoints: Match precipitate colour and excess-NaOH behaviour to the corresponding metal ion

nodes.label: Overall timeline of atmospheric change and its causes
nodes.objective: Describe the main changes in the Earth's atmosphere over geological time and the causes of these changes.
essentialPoints: Sequence: volcanic CO2-rich early atmosphere → ocean/carbonate CO2 removal → photosynthesis producing O2 and removing CO2 → formation of fossil fuel/sedimentary carbon stores → modern stable composition
Combines biological and geological processes as causes of change

nodes.label: Human activities that increase atmospheric carbon dioxide
nodes.objective: Recall two human activities that increase atmospheric carbon dioxide levels.
essentialPoints: Combustion of fossil fuels releases CO2
Deforestation reduces CO2 uptake by photosynthesis and can release stored carbon

nodes.label: Human activities that increase atmospheric methane
nodes.objective: Recall two human activities that increase atmospheric methane levels.
essentialPoints: Livestock farming (e.g. cattle) releases methane through digestion
Rice paddy fields and landfill sites release methane from decomposition

nodes.label: Haber process conditions: catalyst, temperature, pressure
nodes.objective: Recall the catalyst, temperature and pressure used in the Haber process.
essentialPoints: Iron catalyst used
Approximately 450°C and 200 atmospheres pressure

nodes.label: Mining potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock
nodes.objective: State that potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock are obtained by mining.
essentialPoints: Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are mined directly for use as fertilisers
Phosphate rock is mined but cannot be used directly as a fertiliser

nodes.label: Sustainable development
nodes.objective: Define sustainable development and its role in chemistry.
essentialPoints: Development that meets current needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own needs
Chemistry contributes via improved agricultural/industrial processes

nodes.label: Limited nature of metal ore resources (HT)
nodes.objective: State that Earth's metal ore resources are limited and copper ores are becoming scarce.
essentialPoints: Metal ores are a finite resource
High-grade copper ores are becoming scarce

nodes.label: Environmental impact of obtaining raw materials by quarrying/mining
nodes.objective: Describe the environmental impacts of extracting raw materials for metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and plastics.
essentialPoints: Metals, glass, building materials, ceramics and most plastics come from limited raw materials
Quarrying and mining cause environmental impacts (habitat loss, noise, dust, landscape change)

nodes.label: Definition and cause of corrosion
nodes.objective: Define corrosion and identify rusting as an example.
essentialPoints: Corrosion is destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment
Rusting is an example of corrosion specific to iron

nodes.label: Definition of an alloy
nodes.objective: State that most everyday metals are alloys, being mixtures of a metal with other elements.
essentialPoints: Most metals in everyday use are alloys, mixtures designed to improve properties

nodes.label: Soda-lime glass and borosilicate glass
nodes.objective: Describe the composition and production of soda-lime and borosilicate glass.
essentialPoints: Soda-lime glass made by heating sand, sodium carbonate and limestone
Borosilicate glass made from sand and boron trioxide, melts at higher temperature than soda-lime glass

nodes.label: Clay ceramics production
nodes.objective: Describe how clay ceramics, including pottery and bricks, are made.
essentialPoints: Made by shaping wet clay
Then heating in a furnace to harden

nodes.label: Composite materials: matrix and reinforcement
nodes.objective: Recall examples of composite materials and describe their matrix/reinforcement structure.
essentialPoints: Composites consist of a matrix/binder surrounding fibres or fragments of a reinforcement material
Examples include reinforced concrete and fibreglass

nodes.label: Sedimentation producing sludge and effluent
nodes.objective: Describe sedimentation as a stage separating sewage into sludge and effluent.
essentialPoints: Solid particles settle out as sewage sludge
Remaining liquid is effluent

nodes.label: Evaluating risk in practical science and society
nodes.objective: Evaluate risks in practical work and wider society, and explain why perceived risk differs from measured risk.
essentialPoints: Hazards of science-based technologies must be weighed against benefits
Perceived risk can differ from actual/measured risk (voluntary vs imposed, familiar vs unfamiliar, visible vs invisible)

nodes.label: Identifying hazards and reducing risk in practical work
nodes.objective: Identify hazards in practical contexts and suggest methods to reduce the risk of harm.
essentialPoints: Hazards must be identified before carrying out practical work
Risk of harm can be reduced through specific precautions relevant to the hazard

nodes.label: Making and recording measurements using apparatus
nodes.objective: Make and record observations and measurements accurately using a range of apparatus, reading scales correctly.
essentialPoints: Measurements must be read correctly off analogue and digital scales
Measurements should be recorded with appropriate precision and units

nodes.label: Reading measurement scales (volume, mass, temperature)
nodes.objective: Read analogue and digital scales correctly, including measuring cylinders, balances, thermometers and burettes, to the appropriate precision.
essentialPoints: The scale must be read at eye level, taking the meniscus into account for liquids
Readings should be recorded to the precision of the smallest graduation on the instrument

nodes.label: Carrying out filtration to separate an insoluble solid from a liquid
nodes.objective: Set up filter paper and funnel correctly to separate an insoluble solid (residue) from a liquid (filtrate).
essentialPoints: Filter paper is folded and placed in a funnel to trap insoluble solid while liquid passes through
The residue remains on the filter paper and the filtrate is collected below

nodes.label: Measuring pH using indicators or a probe
nodes.objective: Use universal indicator/pH paper or a pH probe correctly to measure and record the pH of a solution.
essentialPoints: Universal indicator or pH paper is compared to a colour chart to estimate pH
A calibrated pH probe gives a more precise numerical pH reading

nodes.label: Interconverting units
nodes.objective: Convert measurements between related units, including using prefixes and standard form.
essentialPoints: Converting units requires knowing the relationship (conversion factor) between them
Prefixes and powers of ten are used to convert between multiples of a base unit

nodes.label: Relating data to hypotheses and reasoned explanations
nodes.objective: Present reasoned explanations relating experimental data to a hypothesis, including comparing competing hypotheses.
essentialPoints: The extent to which data supports or contradicts a hypothesis can be commented on
Where multiple hypotheses exist, data can be used to judge which is better supported

nodes.label: Balanced half equations and ionic equations (HT)
nodes.objective: Write balanced half equations and ionic equations where appropriate (HT only).
essentialPoints: Half equations show electron transfer at an electrode (oxidation or reduction)
Ionic equations show only the species that actually change, omitting spectator ions

nodes.label: Titration technique: using a burette, pipette and indicator to find an end-point
nodes.objective: Carry out an acid-alkali titration accurately using a burette, pipette and indicator to identify the end-point.
essentialPoints: A pipette measures a fixed volume of one solution into a conical flask with indicator
A burette is used to add the second solution dropwise until the indicator changes colour (end-point)
A rough titration followed by accurate concordant titrations improves reliability

nodes.label: Separation technique: filtration
nodes.objective: Describe and explain filtration as a technique for separating an insoluble solid from a liquid.
essentialPoints: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper
Used to obtain residue and filtrate

nodes.label: Separation technique: crystallisation
nodes.objective: Describe and explain crystallisation as a technique for obtaining a solute as solid crystals from a solution.
essentialPoints: A solution is heated to evaporate solvent until saturated, then cooled to form crystals
Used to obtain a soluble salt from its solution

nodes.label: Separation technique: simple distillation
nodes.objective: Describe and explain simple distillation for separating a solvent from a solution.
essentialPoints: Liquid is heated to evaporate the solvent, which is then condensed and collected
Separates a solvent (e.g. water) from dissolved solutes, leaving solute behind

nodes.label: Separation technique: fractional distillation
nodes.objective: Describe and explain fractional distillation for separating a mixture of miscible liquids with different boiling points.
essentialPoints: A fractionating column allows separation of liquids with different boiling points
Vapours condense at different heights/temperatures corresponding to their boiling points

nodes.label: Separation technique: chromatography
nodes.objective: Describe and explain paper chromatography as a technique for separating substances based on differing solubility/affinity for a stationary phase.
essentialPoints: Chromatography separates mixtures based on distribution between a mobile and stationary phase
Different substances travel different distances depending on their attraction to each phase

nodes.label: Bohr's model: electrons in fixed energy levels
nodes.objective: Describe Niels Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model, proposing electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances (energy levels).
essentialPoints: Bohr proposed electrons orbit the nucleus only at specific, fixed distances (energy levels/shells)
Bohr's theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations

nodes.label: Discovery of the proton
nodes.objective: Describe how later experiments showed the nuclear positive charge could be subdivided into protons of equal positive charge.
essentialPoints: Experiments showed the positive charge of the nucleus is made of whole-number units
Each unit of positive charge was named the proton

nodes.label: Size and scale of atoms and nuclei
nodes.objective: State the approximate radius of an atom and of a nucleus, and relate these to standard form and everyday scale.
essentialPoints: Atoms have a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10^-10 m)
A nucleus has a radius less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius (about 1 x 10^-14 m)
Almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus

nodes.label: Ions formed by Groups 1,2,6,7 gain noble gas electronic structure
nodes.objective: State that ions formed from Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas.
essentialPoints: Group 1/2 metals lose electrons to reach noble gas structure
Group 6/7 non-metals gain electrons to reach noble gas structure

nodes.label: Ionic compound as a giant lattice held by electrostatic forces (ionic bonding)
nodes.objective: Define an ionic compound as a giant structure of ions held together by strong electrostatic forces acting in all directions.
essentialPoints: Giant structure of oppositely charged ions
Strong electrostatic forces of attraction act in all directions in the lattice
This is called ionic bonding

nodes.label: Recognising common small molecules from chemical formula
nodes.objective: Recognise common substances that consist of small molecules from their chemical formula.
essentialPoints: Small molecule substances have simple molecular formulae (e.g. H2O, CO2)

nodes.label: Weak intermolecular forces between small molecules vs strong covalent bonds within them
nodes.objective: Explain that small molecular substances have weak intermolecular forces between molecules, distinct from the strong covalent bonds within molecules.
essentialPoints: Intermolecular forces act between separate molecules, not within them
These forces are much weaker than covalent bonds
When melting/boiling, intermolecular forces are overcome, not covalent bonds

nodes.label: Recognising metallic giant structures from bonding diagrams
nodes.objective: Recognise a metallic giant structure from a diagram showing positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
essentialPoints: Diagram shows regular array of positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons

nodes.label: Metals have high melting and boiling points due to strong metallic bonding
nodes.objective: Explain that most metals have high melting and boiling points due to strong metallic bonds throughout the giant structure.
essentialPoints: Metals are giant structures held by strong metallic bonding
Large amounts of energy needed to break many strong metallic bonds

nodes.label: Metal atoms arranged in layers, allowing bending and shaping (malleability/ductility)
nodes.objective: Explain that pure metals can be bent and shaped because their atoms are arranged in layers that can slide over each other.
essentialPoints: Atoms in pure metals arranged in ordered layers
Layers of atoms can slide over one another, allowing bending/shaping

nodes.label: Metals conduct electricity via delocalised electrons carrying charge
nodes.objective: Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity in terms of delocalised electrons carrying charge.
essentialPoints: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the metal structure
These moving electrons carry electrical charge through the metal

nodes.label: Metals conduct thermal energy via delocalised electrons transferring energy
nodes.objective: Explain why metals are good conductors of thermal energy in terms of delocalised electrons transferring energy.
essentialPoints: Delocalised electrons transfer thermal energy through the metal structure

nodes.label: Evaluating the use of nanoparticles for a specified purpose (benefits vs risks)
nodes.objective: Given appropriate information, evaluate the use of nanoparticles for a specified purpose by weighing benefits against risks.
essentialPoints: Weigh advantages (e.g. effectiveness, small quantities needed, specific applications) against risks (e.g. unknown health/environmental effects)
Judgement should be grounded in given information about the specified purpose

nodes.label: The Avogadro constant (HT)
nodes.objective: State that the number of particles in one mole of a substance is the Avogadro constant, 6.02 x 10^23 per mole, and apply this to atoms, molecules and ions.
essentialPoints: The Avogadro constant is 6.02 x 10^23 particles per mole
This applies to atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formulae or equations equally
E.g. one mole of C atoms contains the same number of particles as one mole of CO2 molecules

nodes.label: Calculating moles from mass and mass from moles (HT)
nodes.objective: Use the relative formula mass of a substance to calculate the number of moles in a given mass, and vice versa.
essentialPoints: moles = mass / Mr
mass = moles x Mr

nodes.label: Calculating percentage atom economy
nodes.objective: Calculate the percentage atom economy of a reaction using the balanced equation.
essentialPoints: % atom economy = (Mr of desired product / sum of Mr of all reactants) x 100
Calculated from the balanced symbol equation for the reaction

nodes.label: Deducing an order of reactivity from experimental results
nodes.objective: Use experimental observations of metal reactions to rank metals by reactivity.
essentialPoints: Compare rate/vigour of bubbling, heat produced, or displacement observed
Order metals from most to least reactive based on evidence

nodes.label: Acids react with reactive metals to produce salt and hydrogen
nodes.objective: State that acids react with metals (Mg, Zn, Fe) to form a salt plus hydrogen gas.
essentialPoints: Metal + acid -> salt + hydrogen
Limited to magnesium, zinc and iron with hydrochloric and sulfuric acids

nodes.label: Using the pH scale to identify acidic or alkaline solutions
nodes.objective: Classify a solution as acidic, neutral or alkaline from a given pH value.
essentialPoints: Compare measured/given pH value to 7 to classify solution

nodes.label: Each pH unit decrease = x10 increase in hydrogen ion concentration (HT)
nodes.objective: Describe neutrality and relative acidity in terms of hydrogen ion concentration and pH, including the factor of 10 per unit.
essentialPoints: As pH decreases by 1, H+ concentration increases by a factor of 10
Use this relationship for order-of-magnitude calculations of H+ concentration from pH

nodes.label: Predicting products of electrolysis of aqueous solutions of single ionic compounds
nodes.objective: Predict the products at each electrode for electrolysis of a given aqueous ionic compound solution.
essentialPoints: Apply cathode rule and anode rule together to the given solution
Consider both the dissolved compound's ions and water's ions

nodes.label: Describing preparation of named soluble salts from given information
nodes.objective: Apply the general soluble salt preparation method to describe making a specific named salt.
essentialPoints: Select correct insoluble reactant and acid for the named salt
Sequence the standard steps correctly for that example

nodes.label: Identifying oxidised/reduced species in oxygen-transfer reactions
nodes.objective: Identify which substances are oxidised and reduced (loss/gain of oxygen) in a given reaction.
essentialPoints: Substance losing oxygen is reduced
Substance gaining oxygen is oxidised

nodes.label: Interpreting/evaluating specific metal extraction processes from given information
nodes.objective: Use given data about a metal's reactivity to justify the extraction method used.
essentialPoints: Match extraction method (carbon reduction vs electrolysis) to reactivity position
Interpret unfamiliar process information using reactivity series knowledge

nodes.label: Electrolysis used to extract metals more reactive than carbon
nodes.objective: Explain why electrolysis rather than carbon reduction is used to extract very reactive metals or those that react with carbon.
essentialPoints: Used when metal is too reactive to be displaced by carbon
Used when the metal reacts with carbon itself

nodes.label: Writing ionic (half) equations for displacement reactions (HT)
nodes.objective: Write balanced ionic half equations for metal displacement reactions.
essentialPoints: Show electrons transferred explicitly in half equations
Balance charge and atoms in each half equation

nodes.label: Writing/completing half equations for electrode reactions (HT)
nodes.objective: Write and balance half equations for the reactions occurring at electrodes during electrolysis.
essentialPoints: Cathode half equation shows ions gaining electrons
Anode half equation shows ions losing electrons; balance atoms and charge

nodes.label: Half equations for hydrogen fuel cell electrode reactions (HT)
nodes.objective: Write the half equations for the reactions at each electrode in a hydrogen fuel cell.
essentialPoints: At the negative electrode, hydrogen is oxidised, losing electrons
At the positive electrode, oxygen is reduced, gaining electrons, combining with H+ to form water
Half equations must balance atoms and charge

nodes.label: Analysing temperature-change data from Required practical 4
nodes.objective: Process and plot temperature-change results and identify the reaction type as exothermic or endothermic from the data.
essentialPoints: Calculate temperature change (rise or fall) from readings
Plot variable investigated against temperature change
Classify reaction as exothermic or endothermic from the sign of the temperature change

nodes.label: Evaluating hydrogen fuel cells compared with rechargeable cells and batteries
nodes.objective: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of hydrogen fuel cells relative to rechargeable cells and batteries.
essentialPoints: Fuel cells do not need recharging and can operate continuously while fuel is supplied, unlike batteries that run down or need recharging
Fuel cells avoid using and disposing of toxic heavy-metal-based materials found in some rechargeable batteries
Hydrogen storage, production and infrastructure present practical and safety challenges compared with established battery technology
Fuel cell vehicles/devices tend to be lighter as they do not carry a heavy battery mass, but require a hydrogen supply system

nodes.label: Required practical 5: investigating the effect of concentration on rate (gas volume and turbidity methods)
nodes.objective: Carry out an investigation into how changing concentration affects the rate of reaction, using a gas-volume method and a colour-change/turbidity method, including forming a hypothesis.
essentialPoints: Vary concentration of one reactant while keeping other variables (temperature, volume, other reactant amount) constant
Gas-volume method: measure volume of gas produced at set time intervals using a gas syringe or displacement of water
Turbidity/colour method: time how long it takes for a mark to disappear or colour to change
Form a hypothesis linking concentration to rate before testing it

nodes.label: Explaining the effect of surface area on rate using collision theory
nodes.objective: Use collision theory and surface area to volume ratio to explain why increasing surface area of a solid reactant increases rate.
essentialPoints: Greater surface area to volume ratio exposes more particles of the solid to the other reactant
This increases the frequency of collisions between reacting particles
More frequent successful collisions increases rate

nodes.label: How catalysts work: providing a lower activation energy pathway
nodes.objective: Explain that catalysts increase rate by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
essentialPoints: A catalyst provides a different pathway for the reaction
This alternative pathway has a lower activation energy than the uncatalysed reaction
A lower activation energy means a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react, increasing rate

nodes.label: Identifying catalysts from experimental effects and reaction equations
nodes.objective: Identify a substance as a catalyst by observing that it increases rate of reaction without appearing in the balanced chemical equation.
essentialPoints: A catalyst is identified by its effect of speeding up a reaction while remaining chemically unchanged at the end
It does not appear as a reactant or product in the chemical equation

nodes.label: Building molecular models of alkanes
nodes.objective: Use molecular modelling kits to construct 3D representations of alkane molecules.
essentialPoints: Molecular models represent the 3D arrangement of atoms in alkanes
Building models helps visualise bonding around each carbon atom

nodes.label: Fractional distillation of crude oil (evaporation and condensation)
nodes.objective: Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions using evaporation and condensation, based on differing boiling points.
essentialPoints: Crude oil is heated and vaporised then fed into a fractionating column with a temperature gradient
Hydrocarbons condense at different heights according to their boiling points, separating into fractions
Each fraction contains molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms

nodes.label: Complete combustion of hydrocarbons and balanced equations
nodes.objective: Write balanced equations for complete combustion of hydrocarbons producing carbon dioxide and water, understanding oxidation of carbon and hydrogen.
essentialPoints: Complete combustion oxidises carbon and hydrogen in the fuel
Products of complete combustion are carbon dioxide and water
Balanced symbol equations can be written for combustion given a hydrocarbon formula

nodes.label: Identifying an unknown metal ion from flame test results (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Use an observed flame colour to identify which metal ion is present in a sample.
essentialPoints: Match an observed flame colour to the corresponding metal ion
Consider masking effects when the sample may contain more than one ion

nodes.label: Interpreting flame emission spectroscopy data using a reference spectrum (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Interpret instrumental line-spectrum data given in chart or tabular form, comparing to a reference set to identify metal ions and their concentrations.
essentialPoints: Compare an unknown sample's spectrum/data to a reference spectrum of known ions
Match line positions to identify which ions are present
Line intensity/height can indicate relative concentration

nodes.label: Proportions of gases in today's atmosphere (approx. 80% N2, 20% O2, small proportions of CO2, water vapour, noble gases)
nodes.objective: State the approximate percentages of nitrogen, oxygen and other gases in the Earth's current atmosphere, stable for the last 200 million years.
essentialPoints: Approximately 80% nitrogen and 20% oxygen
Small proportions of CO2, water vapour and noble gases
Composition has been broadly constant for ~200 million years

nodes.label: Combustion products from fuels: CO2, water vapour, CO, SO2, oxides of nitrogen, particulates
nodes.objective: Describe how carbon monoxide, soot (carbon particles), sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen are produced by burning fuels, and predict combustion products given fuel composition and conditions.
essentialPoints: Complete combustion of carbon-containing fuels produces CO2 and water vapour
Incomplete combustion (insufficient oxygen) produces carbon monoxide and/or soot (unburned carbon particles/hydrocarbons)
Sulfur impurities in fuel burn to form sulfur dioxide
High temperatures in combustion cause nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react, forming oxides of nitrogen

nodes.label: Human-caused increase in greenhouse gases linked to global climate change
nodes.objective: State that many scientists, based on peer-reviewed evidence, believe increased human-caused greenhouse gas emissions increase atmospheric surface temperature and cause global climate change.
essentialPoints: Increased greenhouse gas concentrations from human activity increase surface atmospheric temperature
This warming is believed by many scientists (based on peer-reviewed evidence) to cause global climate change

nodes.label: Definition of carbon footprint
nodes.objective: Define carbon footprint as the total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
essentialPoints: Carbon footprint = total CO2 and other greenhouse gases emitted
Measured over the full life cycle of a product, service or event

nodes.label: Cooling, liquefying and recycling in the Haber process
nodes.objective: Describe how ammonia is removed and unreacted gases recycled in the Haber process.
essentialPoints: On cooling, ammonia liquefies and is removed from the mixture
Remaining unreacted hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled back into the reactor

nodes.label: Interpreting graphs of reaction conditions versus rate (HT)
nodes.objective: Interpret graphs showing how temperature and pressure affect the rate of the Haber process reaction.
essentialPoints: Higher temperature and pressure generally increase reaction rate
Read and interpret trends from given graphs of conditions vs rate

nodes.label: Applying dynamic equilibrium to the Haber process (HT)
nodes.objective: Apply the principles of dynamic equilibrium to explain how temperature and pressure affect the position of equilibrium in the Haber process.
essentialPoints: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards fewer gas molecules (more ammonia)
Since the forward reaction is exothermic, increasing temperature shifts equilibrium towards reactants (less ammonia)

nodes.label: Stages of a life cycle assessment (LCA)
nodes.objective: Recall the four stages assessed in a life cycle assessment of a product.
essentialPoints: Extracting and processing raw materials
Manufacturing and packaging
Use and operation during lifetime
Disposal at end of useful life, including transport/distribution at each stage

nodes.label: Phytomining (HT)
nodes.objective: Describe phytomining as a method of extracting metal from low-grade ore using plants.
essentialPoints: Plants absorb metal compounds from soil/low-grade ore
Plants harvested and burned to produce ash containing metal compounds

nodes.label: Bioleaching (HT)
nodes.objective: Describe bioleaching as a method of extracting metal from low-grade ore using bacteria.
essentialPoints: Bacteria produce a leachate solution containing metal compounds from low-grade ore

nodes.label: Reduction, reuse and recycling of materials
nodes.objective: Explain how reduction, reuse and recycling by end users conserve resources and reduce environmental impact.
essentialPoints: Reducing use, reusing and recycling materials reduces the use of limited resources and energy
These practices reduce waste and environmental impact

nodes.label: Setting up experiments to test conditions needed for rusting
nodes.objective: Describe how to set up experiments to test which conditions (air, water) are necessary for rusting.
essentialPoints: Set up test tubes with iron exposed to: air+water, air only (dry), water only (no air, e.g. boiled/oil-sealed)

nodes.label: Bronze and brass compositions and uses
nodes.objective: Recall the composition and a use of bronze and brass.
essentialPoints: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc

nodes.label: Gold alloys and carats
nodes.objective: Describe gold jewellery alloys and calculate gold purity in carats.
essentialPoints: Jewellery gold is usually alloyed with silver, copper and zinc
Carat measures proportion of gold: 24 carat = 100% pure, 18 carat = 75% gold

nodes.label: Types of steel alloy and their properties
nodes.objective: Recall the composition and properties of high carbon steel, low carbon steel and stainless steel.
essentialPoints: High carbon steel is strong but brittle
Low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped
Stainless steels (with chromium and nickel) are hard and corrosion resistant

nodes.label: Aluminium alloys - low density
nodes.objective: Recall that aluminium alloys have low density and a use for this property.
essentialPoints: Aluminium alloys have low density, useful in applications like aircraft manufacture

nodes.label: Comparing physical properties of glass, ceramics, polymers, composites and metals
nodes.objective: Compare quantitatively the physical properties of glass, clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals given appropriate information.
essentialPoints: Use given data (e.g. density, strength, melting point) to compare material classes numerically

nodes.label: Anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge
nodes.objective: Describe anaerobic digestion as treatment of sewage sludge.
essentialPoints: Sludge is broken down by microorganisms without oxygen

nodes.label: Aerobic biological treatment of effluent
nodes.objective: Describe aerobic biological treatment as treatment of effluent.
essentialPoints: Effluent is treated by microorganisms in the presence of oxygen to break down remaining organic matter

nodes.label: Safe use of heating apparatus (Bunsen burner, water bath)
nodes.objective: Set up and safely use a Bunsen burner or water bath to heat substances in practical investigations.
essentialPoints: A Bunsen burner should be used with a yellow (safety) flame when not actively heating and blue flame when heating
A water bath provides gentler, more even heating than a direct flame for temperature-sensitive substances

nodes.label: Setting up electrolysis apparatus
nodes.objective: Correctly set up electrodes, electrolyte and power supply to carry out electrolysis safely and observe products at each electrode.
essentialPoints: Electrodes must be connected to the correct terminals of the power supply and immersed in the electrolyte without touching
Products at each electrode are identified and observed separately

nodes.label: Evaluating methods and validity
nodes.objective: Evaluate whether an experimental method is valid and whether sufficient, precise measurements were taken, suggesting improvements.
essentialPoints: Validity means the method actually tests what it claims to test, with controlled variables
Sufficiency and precision of measurements should be assessed
Improvements can be suggested to address weaknesses in a method

nodes.label: Calculating arithmetic mean and range
nodes.objective: Calculate the arithmetic mean and range of a set of repeated measurements.
essentialPoints: The mean is the sum of values divided by the number of values
The range is the difference between the highest and lowest value in a data set

nodes.label: Using a top-pan balance to measure mass
nodes.objective: Correctly zero (tare) and use a top-pan balance to measure the mass of a substance or container.
essentialPoints: A balance must be tared/zeroed with any container before adding the substance
Readings should be recorded to the precision shown on the balance display

nodes.label: Collecting and measuring gas volume produced in a reaction
nodes.objective: Set up apparatus (e.g. gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder over water) to collect and measure the volume of gas produced over time.
essentialPoints: A gas syringe measures the volume of gas produced directly and accurately
Collection over water can be used for gases that are insoluble in water
Volume readings are taken at fixed time intervals to monitor reaction progress

nodes.label: Carrying out paper chromatography
nodes.objective: Set up and run a paper chromatography experiment, applying samples correctly and calculating Rf values from the result.
essentialPoints: A pencil baseline is used to spot samples above the level of the solvent
The solvent front and spot positions are measured to calculate Rf values

nodes.label: Substituting values into equations with correct units
nodes.objective: Substitute numerical values into algebraic equations using appropriate units for physical quantities.
essentialPoints: Every value substituted must be expressed in consistent units before calculation
The final answer must include the correct unit

nodes.label: Selecting an appropriate separation/purification technique
nodes.objective: Suggest a suitable separation or purification technique for a mixture given information about its components.
essentialPoints: Choice of technique depends on properties of the mixture (solubility, boiling point, particle size, colour)
Different techniques suit different combinations of solid/liquid mixtures

nodes.label: Chadwick's discovery of the neutron
nodes.objective: State that James Chadwick's experimental work provided evidence for neutrons within the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.
essentialPoints: Chadwick's experimental work provided evidence for neutrons in the nucleus
This occurred about 20 years after the nuclear model became accepted

nodes.label: Working out ion charge from group number (Groups 1,2,6,7)
nodes.objective: Deduce the charge on an ion of a Group 1, 2, 6 or 7 element from its group number.
essentialPoints: Group 1 ions are 1+, Group 2 ions are 2+
Group 6 ions are 2-, Group 7 ions are 1-

nodes.label: Structure of sodium chloride (dot-and-cross, ball-and-stick, 2D/3D representations)
nodes.objective: Recognise sodium chloride's structure represented in different diagram forms.
essentialPoints: NaCl represented via dot-and-cross, ball-and-stick, 2D and 3D lattice diagrams
Only NaCl structure required in detail

nodes.label: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points
nodes.objective: Explain why ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points in terms of the strength and number of ionic bonds.
essentialPoints: Giant ionic lattice has strong electrostatic forces in all directions
Large amounts of energy needed to break many strong bonds

nodes.label: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved (free ions), not when solid
nodes.objective: Explain why ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution but not as solids.
essentialPoints: Ions are free to move when molten or dissolved, allowing charge to flow
In solid state ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move

nodes.label: Drawing dot and cross diagrams for named covalent molecules
nodes.objective: Draw dot and cross diagrams for hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane.
essentialPoints: Show shared electron pairs between bonded atoms
Show all outer shell electrons for each atom including lone pairs
Covers H2, Cl2, O2, N2, HCl, H2O, NH3, CH4

nodes.label: Small molecular substances have low melting/boiling points due to weak intermolecular forces
nodes.objective: Explain why substances made of small molecules are usually gases or liquids with low melting and boiling points.
essentialPoints: Only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome to melt/boil
Little energy is needed, giving low melting and boiling points

nodes.label: Small molecular substances do not conduct electricity (no overall charge)
nodes.objective: Explain why substances made of small molecules do not conduct electricity.
essentialPoints: Molecules have no overall electric charge
No free ions or delocalised electrons to carry charge

nodes.label: Alloys are harder than pure metals (distortion of atomic layers)
nodes.objective: Explain why alloys are harder than pure metals in terms of distortion of the layers of atoms.
essentialPoints: Pure metals are too soft for many uses so are mixed with other metals to form alloys
Different sized atoms in an alloy distort the regular layers
Distorted layers cannot slide over each other as easily, making alloys harder

nodes.label: Interpreting balanced equations in terms of moles (HT)
nodes.objective: Interpret the balancing numbers of a symbol equation as relative numbers of moles of each substance reacting/produced.
essentialPoints: The balancing number in front of a formula gives the number of moles of that substance in the reaction
E.g. Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2 means 1 mol Mg reacts with 2 mol HCl to give 1 mol MgCl2 and 1 mol H2

nodes.label: Molar volume of a gas at RTP (HT, chemistry only)
nodes.objective: State that equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions, and that one mole of any gas at RTP occupies 24 dm3.
essentialPoints: Equal numbers of moles of any gas occupy the same volume at the same temperature and pressure
One mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20°C, 1 atm) has a volume of 24 dm3

nodes.label: Concentration of solutions in g/dm3
nodes.objective: Define concentration as mass of solute per given volume of solution (e.g. g/dm3) and calculate mass of solute from concentration and volume.
essentialPoints: Concentration measures mass of solute per unit volume of solution, e.g. g/dm3
mass of solute = concentration x volume of solution

nodes.label: Concentration of solutions in mol/dm3 (HT, chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Define concentration measured in mol/dm3 and convert between moles, mass, volume and concentration.
essentialPoints: Concentration in mol/dm3 = moles of solute / volume of solution in dm3
Mass of solute can be found from moles (using Mr) once amount in mol is known

nodes.label: Evaluating which reaction pathway to use (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain why a particular reaction pathway is chosen to produce a specified product, using data such as atom economy, yield, rate, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products.
essentialPoints: A high atom economy and high percentage yield reduce waste and cost, favouring a pathway
A fast rate and a favourable equilibrium position (high product proportion) make a pathway more viable
Useful by-products can improve the overall economics/sustainability of a pathway even if atom economy for one product is lower

nodes.label: Acid-metal reactions as redox reactions in terms of electrons (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain acid-metal reactions as redox in terms of electron gain/loss and identify oxidised/reduced species.
essentialPoints: Metal atoms lose electrons (oxidised) forming metal ions
Hydrogen ions gain electrons (reduced) forming hydrogen gas

nodes.label: Required Practical 3: investigating electrolysis of aqueous solutions
nodes.objective: Investigate the products formed at each electrode when aqueous solutions are electrolysed using inert electrodes, developing a hypothesis.
essentialPoints: Form a hypothesis about expected electrode products before testing
Use gas tests to identify products formed at each electrode

nodes.label: Large energy demand of electrolytic metal extraction
nodes.objective: State that electrolysis requires large amounts of energy to melt compounds and generate the electric current.
essentialPoints: Energy needed to melt the ionic compound
Energy needed to produce the electrical current

nodes.label: Aluminium extraction by electrolysis of molten Al2O3/cryolite mixture
nodes.objective: Describe the electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite with carbon anodes.
essentialPoints: Aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite as the electrolyte
Carbon is used as the positive electrode (anode)

nodes.label: Identifying oxidised/reduced species from electron transfer (HT)
nodes.objective: Identify which species are oxidised and reduced in a given equation or half equation using electron transfer.
essentialPoints: Species losing electrons is oxidised
Species gaining electrons is reduced

nodes.label: Cathode = reduction, anode = oxidation in electrolysis half equations (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain that electrode half equations show reduction at the cathode and oxidation at the anode, e.g. 2H+ + 2e- -> H2 and 4OH- -> O2 + 2H2O + 4e-.
essentialPoints: Positive ions gain electrons at the cathode (reduction)
Negative ions lose electrons at the anode (oxidation)

nodes.label: Evaluating uses and applications of exothermic and endothermic reactions
nodes.objective: Given information, evaluate the suitability of exothermic or endothermic reactions for a given application.
essentialPoints: Weigh practical factors (cost, reliability, controllability, safety) against the temperature change achieved
Judge suitability of a reaction for a stated everyday use using given data

nodes.label: Calculating and comparing rates of reaction from required practical 5 data
nodes.objective: Use data collected from required practical 5 to calculate rate of reaction and compare rates across different concentrations.
essentialPoints: Use mean rate formula on collected volume/time or 1/time data to calculate rate
Compare calculated rates across concentrations to test the hypothesis

nodes.label: Using proportionality to describe how a factor affects rate
nodes.objective: Apply simple ideas about proportionality when using collision theory to explain the effect of a factor on rate.
essentialPoints: A factor increasing collision frequency or energy is described using proportional relationships (e.g. doubling concentration approximately doubling collision frequency)

nodes.label: Drawing a reaction profile for a catalysed reaction
nodes.objective: Draw a reaction profile showing both the catalysed and uncatalysed pathways, with the catalysed pathway having a lower activation energy peak.
essentialPoints: The reaction profile shows two curves from the same reactants to the same products
The catalysed pathway has a lower peak (activation energy) than the uncatalysed pathway
The overall energy change between reactants and products is the same for both pathways

nodes.label: Fractions as fuels and petrochemical feedstock
nodes.objective: State that fractions from crude oil are processed into fuels (petrol, diesel, kerosene, heavy fuel oil, LPG) and feedstock for petrochemicals (solvents, lubricants, polymers, detergents).
essentialPoints: Fractions are processed to make fuels such as petrol, diesel, kerosene, heavy fuel oil and LPG
Fractions also provide feedstock for the petrochemical industry to make solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents

nodes.label: Combining chemical tests to identify the ions in an unknown ionic compound (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Use flame tests, hydroxide precipitation, carbonate, halide and sulfate tests together to deduce the full identity of an unknown ionic compound.
essentialPoints: Systematically apply relevant tests (cation and anion) to narrow down the compound's identity
Combine results from multiple tests since a single test alone rarely gives a unique identification

nodes.label: Advantages of instrumental methods compared with the chemical tests in this specification (chemistry only)
nodes.objective: Compare instrumental methods with manual chemical tests and state their advantages.
essentialPoints: Instrumental methods are faster than manual chemical tests
Instrumental methods are more sensitive, detecting very small quantities
Instrumental methods are more accurate and reduce reliance on subjective colour judgement
Chemical tests require larger sample amounts and skilled visual interpretation, which instrumental methods avoid

nodes.label: Carbon monoxide: a toxic, colourless, odourless gas
nodes.objective: Describe carbon monoxide as a toxic gas that is colourless and odourless, making it hard to detect, and explain the danger this poses to humans.
essentialPoints: Carbon monoxide is toxic to humans (binds to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport)
It is colourless and odourless, so cannot easily be detected without specific alarms

nodes.label: Effects of sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen: respiratory problems and acid rain
nodes.objective: Describe and explain how sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.
essentialPoints: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen irritate the respiratory system, worsening conditions such as asthma
These gases dissolve in atmospheric water droplets forming acidic solutions, which fall as acid rain
Acid rain damages plants, aquatic ecosystems and buildings/structures

nodes.label: Effects of particulates: global dimming and health problems
nodes.objective: Describe and explain how particulates (soot and unburned hydrocarbons) cause global dimming and health problems for humans.
essentialPoints: Particulates reflect sunlight back into space and provide surfaces for cloud droplet formation, contributing to global dimming (reduced sunlight reaching Earth's surface)
Fine particulates can be inhaled deep into the lungs, causing respiratory and cardiovascular health problems

nodes.label: Evaluating evidence quality and uncertainty in climate change reports
nodes.objective: Evaluate the quality of evidence in a report about global climate change, describe uncertainties in the evidence base, and recognise the importance of peer review and communication of results.
essentialPoints: Complex systems like global climate are difficult to model, leading to simplified models with inherent uncertainty
Media presentations may be based on partial evidence and can be biased
Peer review validates scientific claims before wide acceptance; communicating results to varied audiences is important

nodes.label: Potential effects of global climate change
nodes.objective: Describe briefly four potential effects of global climate change.
essentialPoints: Sea level rise from melting ice caps/glaciers and thermal expansion, causing flooding
Changes to weather patterns causing more frequent/severe storms
Changes in distribution of wildlife species (migration, habitat loss)
Changes to amount/timing/distribution of rainfall, affecting agriculture and water supply

nodes.label: Actions to reduce carbon footprint
nodes.objective: Describe actions that can reduce emissions of carbon dioxide and methane, thereby reducing carbon footprint.
essentialPoints: Using renewable/alternative energy sources instead of fossil fuels reduces CO2 emissions
Improving energy efficiency and carbon capture/storage reduces emissions
Reducing meat consumption and changes to waste management/farming practices reduce methane emissions

nodes.label: Ammonia used to make ammonium salts and nitric acid
nodes.objective: State that ammonia produced by the Haber process is used to manufacture ammonium salts and nitric acid.
essentialPoints: Ammonia reacts with acids to form ammonium salts
Ammonia is oxidised industrially to produce nitric acid

nodes.label: Trade-off between rate of production and equilibrium yield (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain the trade-off between rate of production and position of equilibrium in the Haber process.
essentialPoints: High temperature increases rate but reduces equilibrium yield of ammonia (shifts equilibrium backwards)
A compromise temperature balances a reasonable rate against acceptable yield

nodes.label: LCA is not purely objective
nodes.objective: Explain why LCA is not a purely objective process.
essentialPoints: Use of water, resources, energy and some wastes can be quantified fairly easily
Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires subjective value judgements

nodes.label: Obtaining copper from leachate/ash solutions by displacement or electrolysis (HT)
nodes.objective: Describe how copper metal is obtained from solutions of copper compounds produced by phytomining or bioleaching.
essentialPoints: Displacement using scrap iron (more reactive metal displaces copper)
Electrolysis of the copper solution can also extract copper

nodes.label: Reuse of glass bottles
nodes.objective: Describe how glass bottles can be reused or recycled by crushing and melting.
essentialPoints: Some glass bottles are reused directly
Glass can be crushed and melted to make different glass products

nodes.label: Recycling of metals by melting and reforming
nodes.objective: Describe how metals are recycled and how the required degree of separation varies.
essentialPoints: Metals recycled by melting and recasting or reforming into different products
Amount of separation needed depends on the material and properties required of the final product
Scrap steel can be added to iron from a blast furnace to reduce the amount of new ore needed

nodes.label: Interpreting rusting experiment results: air and water both required
nodes.objective: Interpret comparative rusting experiment results to conclude that both air and water are necessary for rusting.
essentialPoints: Rust only forms in the tube where iron is exposed to both air and water
Absence of rust in the air-only or water-only (no air) tubes shows both substances are required

nodes.label: Interpreting and evaluating composition and uses of unfamiliar alloys
nodes.objective: Interpret and evaluate the composition and uses of alloys other than those specified, given appropriate information.
essentialPoints: Relate given alloy composition/percentages to likely properties
Judge suitability of an alloy for a stated use based on given data

nodes.label: Selecting materials for a use based on their properties
nodes.objective: Explain how the properties of materials relate to their uses and select appropriate materials given information.
essentialPoints: Match required properties (strength, density, melting point, corrosion resistance) to an appropriate material
Justify material choice using its specific properties

nodes.label: Comparing ease of obtaining potable water from waste, ground and salt water
nodes.objective: Comment on the relative ease of obtaining potable water from waste water, ground water and salt water.
essentialPoints: Ground water requires least treatment (filtration + sterilisation)
Waste water requires extensive treatment (screening, sedimentation, digestion, aerobic treatment) before further purification
Salt water requires energy-intensive desalination, making it hardest/most costly

nodes.label: Monitoring temperature change during a reaction
nodes.objective: Use a thermometer or temperature probe correctly to monitor and record temperature changes during a chemical reaction.
essentialPoints: The thermometer bulb/probe should be immersed fully in the reacting mixture without touching the container
The maximum or minimum temperature change is recorded relative to the starting temperature

nodes.label: Uncertainty in measurements: range and mean as estimates
nodes.objective: Represent the distribution of results and use the range about a mean as a measure of uncertainty.
essentialPoints: Every measurement has some uncertainty
The mean of repeat readings is a best estimate of the true value
The range of repeat readings about the mean can be used as a measure of uncertainty

nodes.label: Preparing solutions of known concentration
nodes.objective: Accurately prepare a solution of known concentration by dissolving a known mass of solute in a known volume of solvent, or by dilution.
essentialPoints: A known mass of solute is dissolved and made up to a precise volume using a volumetric flask
Dilution reduces concentration by a calculable factor when a stock solution is diluted with a known volume of solvent

nodes.label: Relative electrical charges of protons, neutrons and electrons
nodes.objective: State the relative charges of protons (+1), neutrons (0) and electrons (-1).
essentialPoints: Protons have a relative charge of +1
Neutrons have a relative charge of 0
Electrons have a relative charge of -1

nodes.label: Drawing dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds
nodes.objective: Draw dot and cross diagrams showing electron transfer for ionic compounds formed from Group 1/2 metals with Group 6/7 non-metals.
essentialPoints: Diagram shows electron transfer from metal to non-metal
Ions shown with square brackets and charges
Only outer shell electrons are shown

nodes.label: Deducing a compound is ionic from a structural diagram
nodes.objective: Identify that a given structure diagram represents an ionic compound.
essentialPoints: Recognise repeating lattice pattern of alternating ions as ionic

nodes.label: Limitations of dot-and-cross/ball-and-stick/2D/3D models for giant ionic structures
nodes.objective: Describe the limitations of different representations of giant ionic lattices.
essentialPoints: Ball-and-stick implies fixed bonds/gaps not present in reality
2D diagrams cannot show the full 3D extent of the lattice
No single model shows relative sizes, scale or that forces act in all directions

nodes.label: Representing covalent bonds using lines (single bonds) in molecules, polymers and giant structures
nodes.objective: Represent covalent bonds using a line to show a single bond in small molecules, polymer repeating units and giant covalent structures.
essentialPoints: A line represents one shared pair of electrons (single covalent bond)
Used for small molecules, polymer repeat units and giant structures

nodes.label: Intermolecular forces (and mp/bp) increase with molecule size
nodes.objective: Explain the trend that larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces and therefore higher melting and boiling points.
essentialPoints: Intermolecular forces increase in strength as molecule size increases
Larger molecules therefore have higher melting and boiling points

nodes.label: Calculating reacting masses from balanced equations (HT)
nodes.objective: Calculate masses of reactants and products from a balanced symbol equation and a given mass of one substance.
essentialPoints: Convert given mass to moles using Mr
Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to find moles of the other substance
Convert moles back to mass using Mr of that substance

nodes.label: Calculating the volume of a gas from its mass and Mr (HT)
nodes.objective: Calculate the volume of a gas at room temperature and pressure from its mass and relative formula mass using the molar volume.
essentialPoints: Convert mass to moles using Mr
Multiply moles by 24 dm3 to obtain volume at RTP

nodes.label: Calculating gas volumes from a balanced equation (HT)
nodes.objective: Calculate volumes of gaseous reactants or products from a balanced equation and a given volume of a gaseous reactant or product.
essentialPoints: Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation directly with gas volumes (since equal moles of gas occupy equal volumes at fixed conditions)
Given volume of one gas can be scaled by the ratio to find the volume of another gas

nodes.label: Relating mass of solute, volume of solution and concentration (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain how the mass of solute and the volume of solution together determine the concentration of a solution.
essentialPoints: Increasing mass of solute in a fixed volume increases concentration
Increasing volume for a fixed mass of solute decreases concentration

nodes.label: Explaining why a mixture (with cryolite) is used as the electrolyte
nodes.objective: Explain that cryolite lowers the melting point of aluminium oxide, reducing energy costs.
essentialPoints: Cryolite lowers the melting point of the mixture compared to pure aluminium oxide
This reduces the energy needed to melt the electrolyte

nodes.label: Explaining why the positive electrode must be continually replaced
nodes.objective: Explain that the carbon anode reacts with oxygen produced, burning away and needing replacement.
essentialPoints: Oxygen produced at the anode reacts with the hot carbon electrode
Carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide, gradually wearing the anode away

nodes.label: Evaluating the required practical 5 method and identifying improvements
nodes.objective: Identify sources of error in the concentration-rate investigation and suggest improvements to the method.
essentialPoints: Judging the disappearance of a mark or a colour change by eye introduces subjective/random error
Gas leaks or delay in starting the timer affect gas-volume measurements systematically
Improvements include using light sensors/data loggers for objectivity and repeating readings

nodes.label: Trends in boiling point, viscosity and flammability with molecular size
nodes.objective: Recall how boiling point, viscosity and flammability of hydrocarbons change as molecular size increases, and relate this to their use as fuels.
essentialPoints: Boiling point increases with increasing molecular size
Viscosity increases with increasing molecular size
Flammability decreases with increasing molecular size
These properties determine suitability of different fractions as fuels

nodes.label: Discussing scale, risk and environmental implications of global climate change
nodes.objective: Discuss the scale, risk and environmental implications associated with global climate change.
essentialPoints: Global scale of climate change means impacts are widespread and interconnected across ecosystems and economies
Risk assessment weighs likelihood and severity of effects (e.g. flooding, food/water insecurity) against uncertainty in predictions
Environmental implications include biodiversity loss and habitat disruption alongside human socioeconomic impacts

nodes.label: Treating phosphate rock with acids to make soluble salts
nodes.objective: Recall the names of the salts produced when phosphate rock is treated with nitric, sulfuric and phosphoric acid.
essentialPoints: Phosphate rock + nitric acid produces phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate
Phosphate rock + sulfuric acid produces single superphosphate (calcium sulfate and calcium phosphate)
Phosphate rock + phosphoric acid produces triple superphosphate (calcium phosphate)

nodes.label: Justifying commercial conditions used in the Haber process (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain how the commercially used conditions for the Haber process relate to availability/cost of raw materials and energy, and control of rate and equilibrium.
essentialPoints: 200 atm balances increased yield/rate against high cost of generating and containing very high pressure
450°C balances a reasonably fast rate against not sacrificing too much yield, while limiting energy costs

nodes.label: Misuse of selective/abbreviated LCAs
nodes.objective: Explain how selective or abbreviated LCAs can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions.
essentialPoints: Selective/abbreviated LCAs can be devised to support a particular conclusion
This can be misused for advertising or marketing purposes

nodes.label: Carrying out and interpreting a comparative LCA (e.g. plastic vs paper bags)
nodes.objective: Carry out simple comparative LCAs for products such as plastic and paper shopping bags, using appropriate data.
essentialPoints: Compare the four LCA stages between two competing products
Quantify only where data is readily available for energy, water, resources and waste
Draw conclusions on overall environmental impact based on available evidence

nodes.label: Evaluating biological methods of metal extraction (HT)
nodes.objective: Evaluate phytomining and bioleaching as alternatives to traditional mining, given appropriate information.
essentialPoints: Avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock, reducing environmental impact
Slower processes than traditional mining and yield smaller quantities of metal
Allow use of otherwise uneconomic low-grade ores, extending resource availability

nodes.label: Evaluating ways of reducing use of limited resources
nodes.objective: Evaluate reduction, reuse and recycling strategies given appropriate information.
essentialPoints: Reuse saves more energy than recycling as no reprocessing is needed
Recycling still requires energy for collection, sorting and reprocessing but far less than extracting new raw material
Effectiveness depends on availability of collection/sorting infrastructure and market for recycled material

nodes.label: Barrier methods of preventing corrosion
nodes.objective: Describe barrier methods of preventing corrosion such as greasing, painting and electroplating.
essentialPoints: Coatings like grease, paint or electroplating act as a barrier excluding air and water
Aluminium naturally forms a protective oxide coating preventing further corrosion

nodes.label: Accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility
nodes.objective: Distinguish between accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility when evaluating data.
essentialPoints: An accurate measurement is close to the true value
Precise measurements cluster closely together
Repeatable results are obtained by the same investigator using the same method and equipment
Reproducible results are obtained by different investigators or different equipment

nodes.label: Titration procedure for reacting volumes of strong acid and strong alkali
nodes.objective: Describe how to carry out a titration to accurately find reacting volumes of a strong acid and strong alkali.
essentialPoints: Alkali (or acid) measured by pipette into flask with indicator
Acid added from burette until indicator shows endpoint; repeat for concordant results

nodes.label: Atomic number and neutral atoms
nodes.objective: Explain that atoms have no overall charge because protons equal electrons, and define atomic number.
essentialPoints: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons
Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom of an element
All atoms of a given element have the same number of protons; different elements have different numbers of protons

nodes.label: Relative masses of protons, neutrons and electrons
nodes.objective: State the relative masses of a proton, neutron and electron.
essentialPoints: Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1
Electrons have a relative mass that is very small (about 1/1835), often treated as negligible

nodes.label: Working out empirical formula of an ionic compound from a model/diagram
nodes.objective: Determine the empirical formula of an ionic compound by counting ions shown in a model or diagram.
essentialPoints: Count ratio of each type of ion shown in the diagram
Express as simplest whole-number ratio (empirical formula)

nodes.label: Representing polymers with repeating unit notation (n)
nodes.objective: Represent polymer structures using a repeating unit in brackets with subscript n.
essentialPoints: Polymers shown as a repeat unit in brackets with n outside
n represents a large number of repeat units

nodes.label: Giant covalent structures are solids with very high melting points
nodes.objective: Explain that giant covalent structures have very high melting points because strong covalent bonds throughout the structure must be overcome.
essentialPoints: All atoms linked by strong covalent bonds throughout the structure
These bonds must be broken (not just weak intermolecular forces) to melt/boil
Examples: diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide

nodes.label: Deriving balancing numbers from reacting masses (HT)
