nodes.objective: Balance an equation given the masses of reactants and products by converting masses to moles and moles to a simple whole-number ratio.
essentialPoints: Convert each given mass to moles using Mr
Divide each mole value by the smallest to obtain a simple ratio
Use this ratio as the balancing numbers in the equation

nodes.label: Limiting reactants (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain the effect of a limiting reactant on the amount of product obtainable, in terms of moles or masses.
essentialPoints: An excess of one reactant is often used to ensure the other reacts completely
The reactant completely used up is the limiting reactant
The limiting reactant determines the maximum amount of product that can form

nodes.label: Calculating theoretical yield from a given mass of reactant (HT)
nodes.objective: Calculate the theoretical mass of a product from a given mass of reactant using the balanced equation.
essentialPoints: Uses the same mole-ratio method as reacting mass calculations
Gives the maximum possible mass of product assuming complete conversion

nodes.label: Explaining how concentration in mol/dm3 relates to mass of solute and volume (HT)
nodes.objective: Explain how the concentration of a solution in mol/dm3 depends on both the mass (via moles) of solute and the volume of solution.
essentialPoints: Concentration increases if more moles of solute are dissolved in the same volume
Concentration decreases if the same amount of solute is dissolved in a larger volume
Relates mass, Mr and volume together via moles per dm3

nodes.label: Investigating properties of different hydrocarbons
nodes.objective: Carry out practical comparisons of viscosity, flammability and boiling point for hydrocarbon samples of different chain length.
essentialPoints: Compare viscosity by timing flow of samples
Compare flammability by testing ease of ignition
Compare boiling points using heating and thermometer readings

nodes.label: Cracking: catalytic cracking and steam cracking
nodes.objective: Describe cracking as breaking down larger hydrocarbons into smaller molecules, and describe the general conditions for catalytic and steam cracking.
essentialPoints: Cracking breaks larger hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful molecules
Catalytic cracking uses a catalyst and high temperature
Steam cracking uses a high temperature and steam without a catalyst

nodes.label: Reasons why actions to reduce carbon footprint may be limited
nodes.objective: Give reasons why actions to reduce carbon dioxide and methane emissions may be limited.
essentialPoints: Economic costs of alternative technologies can be high, and may disadvantage individuals, businesses or countries
Lack of public/political will or international agreement can limit government action
Incomplete science or lack of international cooperation can limit effectiveness of proposed solutions
Lifestyle changes are difficult to implement/enforce on a large scale

nodes.label: Sacrificial protection and galvanising
nodes.objective: Explain sacrificial protection, including galvanising, in terms of relative reactivity.
essentialPoints: A more reactive metal (e.g. zinc) is applied to protect iron; it corrodes preferentially
Galvanising coats iron with zinc, providing both a barrier and sacrificial protection
The more reactive metal loses electrons in preference to the protected metal

nodes.label: Random error, systematic error and anomalous results
nodes.objective: Identify potential sources of random and systematic error, and explain how to treat anomalous values.
essentialPoints: Random error causes results to vary unpredictably and can be reduced by taking more measurements and finding a mean
Systematic error causes results to differ from the true value by a consistent amount each time
Anomalous values should be investigated and, if due to poor measurement, discarded

nodes.label: Calculating unknown concentration from titration results (HT)
nodes.objective: Determine the concentration of one solution in mol/dm3 and g/dm3 from titration reacting volumes and the known concentration of the other solution.
essentialPoints: Use the known concentration and volume to find moles of the known solution reacted
Use the balanced equation's mole ratio to find moles of the unknown solution
Divide by its volume to find concentration in mol/dm3, then convert to g/dm3 using Mr

nodes.label: Calculating concentrations from titration data (mol/dm3 and g/dm3) (HT)
nodes.objective: Calculate the concentration of a solution in mol/dm3 and g/dm3 using titration results.
essentialPoints: Use moles = concentration x volume for the known solution to find moles reacted
Use reaction stoichiometry to find moles of unknown, then convert to mol/dm3 and g/dm3

nodes.label: Required practical: preparing an ammonium salt
nodes.objective: Prepare an ammonium salt in the laboratory by reacting ammonia solution with an acid.
essentialPoints: Titrate ammonia solution with acid using indicator to find volume needed for neutralisation
Repeat without indicator using the neutralisation volume, then evaporate and crystallise to obtain the pure ammonium salt

nodes.label: Electronic structure of atoms (energy levels/shells)
nodes.objective: Represent the electronic structure of the first 20 elements using numbers or diagrams, with electrons filling the lowest available energy levels.
essentialPoints: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels (shells) first
Electronic structure can be written as numbers (e.g. 2,8,1 for sodium) or shown as a diagram
Shells fill in order: 2, then 8, then 8 (for the first 20 elements)

nodes.label: Mass number
nodes.objective: Define mass number as the sum of protons and neutrons in an atom.
essentialPoints: Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons

nodes.label: Recognising substances as small molecules, polymers or giant covalent structures from bonding diagrams
nodes.objective: Classify a substance as a small molecule, polymer or giant covalent structure from a diagram of its bonding.
essentialPoints: Small molecules show a fixed small number of atoms bonded together
Polymers show a repeating unit with n
Giant covalent structures show an extended repeating network

nodes.label: Polymers are solids at room temperature due to strong covalent bonds and relatively strong intermolecular forces
nodes.objective: Explain why polymers are solid at room temperature, referencing bonding within and between polymer chains.
essentialPoints: Atoms within polymer molecules linked by strong covalent bonds
Intermolecular forces between long polymer chains are relatively strong (compared to small molecules)
Combined effect makes polymers solid at room temperature

nodes.label: Recognising giant covalent structures from diagrams of bonding and structure
nodes.objective: Recognise a giant covalent structure from a diagram showing an extended network of covalently bonded atoms.
essentialPoints: Identify a repeating extended network with no separate molecules as giant covalent

nodes.label: Diamond structure: each carbon forms 4 covalent bonds in a giant covalent lattice
nodes.objective: Describe the structure of diamond as each carbon atom forming four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant lattice.
essentialPoints: Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds to other carbon atoms
Forms a rigid giant covalent structure

nodes.label: Graphite structure: each carbon forms 3 covalent bonds in hexagonal layers, one delocalised electron per atom
nodes.objective: Describe the structure of graphite as layers of hexagonal rings with three covalent bonds per carbon atom and one delocalised electron per atom, with no bonds between layers.
essentialPoints: Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms
Forms layers of hexagonal rings
No covalent bonds exist between the layers
One electron per carbon atom is delocalised

nodes.label: Products of cracking: alkanes and alkenes; balancing cracking equations
nodes.objective: Identify that cracking produces both alkanes and alkenes and balance equations representing cracking reactions given formulae.
essentialPoints: Cracking produces smaller alkanes and alkenes from larger alkane molecules
Equations for cracking can be balanced given reactant and product formulae

nodes.label: Evaluating data quality to suggest improvements
nodes.objective: Use accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility and error types to evaluate data and suggest improvements to procedures.
essentialPoints: Evaluating data quality requires combining knowledge of accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility and error type
Suggested improvements should target the specific identified source of error or imprecision

nodes.label: Carrying out an acid-base titration using a burette
nodes.objective: Use a burette, pipette and indicator to accurately measure the volume of solution needed to reach an end point in a titration.
essentialPoints: A pipette delivers a fixed, accurate volume of one solution into a conical flask
A burette is used to add the second solution gradually, reading the volume at the meniscus to the nearest graduation
An indicator is used to identify the end point of the reaction
Repeat titrations should be carried out until concordant results (within 0.10 cm3) are obtained

nodes.label: Required Practical 2: titration of strong acid and strong alkali
nodes.objective: Carry out a titration to determine reacting volumes and calculate concentration of a solution.
essentialPoints: Follow titration procedure to obtain concordant titre volumes
Use results with known concentration to calculate unknown concentration (HT)

nodes.label: Comparing industrial and laboratory preparation of fertiliser compounds
nodes.objective: Compare the industrial production of fertilisers with laboratory preparation of the same compounds, given appropriate information.
essentialPoints: Industrial production uses continuous processes, bulk raw materials and requires cost/safety/environmental control at large scale
Laboratory preparation is batch-based, small-scale and uses simpler apparatus, without the same economic constraints

nodes.label: Arrangement of the periodic table by atomic number and groups
nodes.objective: Describe how elements are arranged in the periodic table by atomic number into periods and groups of similar properties.
essentialPoints: Elements are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number
Elements with similar properties are placed in the same column (group)
Similar properties recur at regular intervals, giving the table its 'periodic' name

nodes.label: Isotopes
nodes.objective: Define isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
essentialPoints: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same proton number) with different numbers of neutrons
Isotopes therefore have different mass numbers

nodes.label: Limitations of dot-and-cross/ball-and-stick/2D/3D models for molecules and giant covalent structures
nodes.objective: Describe the limitations of different representations of covalent molecules and giant structures.
essentialPoints: Ball-and-stick models exaggerate bond lengths/gaps between atoms
2D diagrams cannot show true 3D shape or bond angles
Models do not show relative sizes of atoms accurately

nodes.label: Deducing molecular formula from a model or diagram of a molecule
nodes.objective: Deduce the molecular formula of a substance from a model or diagram showing its atoms and bonds.
essentialPoints: Count the number of each type of atom shown in the diagram/model

nodes.label: Recognising polymers from diagrams of bonding and structure
nodes.objective: Recognise a polymer from a diagram showing its repeating unit and bonding.
essentialPoints: Identify repeating unit notation and long chain structure as a polymer

nodes.label: Explaining diamond's properties (very hard, very high mp, non-conductor) from its structure
nodes.objective: Explain the properties of diamond (hardness, high melting point, non-conductivity) in terms of its structure and bonding.
essentialPoints: Very hard because many strong covalent bonds resist deformation in all directions
Very high melting point because many strong covalent bonds must be broken
Does not conduct electricity because there are no free electrons or ions

nodes.label: Explaining graphite's properties (soft/slippery, conducts electricity, high mp) from its structure
nodes.objective: Explain the properties of graphite (softness, electrical conductivity, high melting point) in terms of its layered structure and delocalised electrons.
essentialPoints: Layers can slide over each other as there are no covalent bonds between layers, making graphite soft/slippery
Delocalised electrons allow graphite to conduct electricity, similar to metals
High melting point because strong covalent bonds within layers must be broken

nodes.label: Graphene as a single layer of graphite
nodes.objective: Describe graphene as a single layer of graphite, one atom thick.
essentialPoints: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal rings
It is essentially one layer of graphite

nodes.label: Fullerenes: hollow carbon molecules based on hexagonal (plus 5/7) rings, e.g. Buckminsterfullerene C60
nodes.objective: Describe fullerenes as hollow-shaped carbon molecules based on hexagonal rings, sometimes including five- or seven-membered rings.
essentialPoints: Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes
Structure based mainly on hexagonal rings, may include rings of five or seven carbons
Buckminsterfullerene (C60) was the first fullerene discovered, with a spherical shape

nodes.label: Bromine water test for alkenes
nodes.objective: Recall that bromine water changes from orange to colourless in the presence of an alkene, used as a test for unsaturation.
essentialPoints: Bromine water is orange and turns colourless when shaken with an alkene
This distinguishes alkenes (unsaturated) from alkanes (saturated), which do not decolourise it

nodes.label: Usefulness of cracking: meeting fuel demand and supplying alkenes for chemicals
nodes.objective: Explain why cracking is useful, given high demand for small-molecule fuels and demand for alkenes for polymers and other chemicals.
essentialPoints: There is high demand for fuels with small molecules, more than crude oil naturally yields
Cracking converts less useful larger hydrocarbons into more useful smaller alkanes for fuel
Cracking produces alkenes used to manufacture polymers and other chemicals

nodes.label: Alkenes: general formula CnH2n and the C=C double bond
nodes.objective: State the general formula for alkenes, define unsaturation, and name/recognise the first four alkenes from formulae or diagrams.
essentialPoints: Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C)
General formula for alkenes is CnH2n
Alkenes are unsaturated, having two fewer hydrogens than the corresponding alkane
First four alkenes are ethene, propene, butene and pentene

nodes.label: Communicating scientific rationale, methods, findings and conclusions
nodes.objective: Present coherent, logically structured reports of investigations covering rationale, method, findings and conclusions.
essentialPoints: A scientific report should logically link rationale, method, findings and conclusion
Findings should be communicated using verbal, diagrammatic, graphical, numerical or symbolic forms as appropriate

nodes.label: Groups and outer-shell electrons determine chemical properties
nodes.objective: Explain that elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons, giving them similar chemical properties, and relate group/period position to electronic structure and atomic number.
essentialPoints: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons
This shared outer electron number causes similar chemical properties
Position in the periodic table can be explained by/predicted from electronic structure and atomic number

nodes.label: Calculating numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms/ions
nodes.objective: Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion given its atomic number and mass number.
essentialPoints: Number of protons = atomic number
Number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number
Number of electrons = number of protons ± charge for ions

nodes.label: Relative atomic mass from isotopic abundance
nodes.objective: Calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from the percentage abundances of its isotopes.
essentialPoints: Relative atomic mass is a weighted average accounting for isotope abundance
Calculated as sum of (isotope mass x % abundance) / 100

nodes.label: Explaining graphene's properties and uses in electronics and composites
nodes.objective: Explain the properties of graphene in terms of its structure and bonding and relate these to its uses in electronics and composites.
essentialPoints: Delocalised electrons make graphene an excellent electrical conductor
Strong covalent bonds in a single layer make it strong yet very thin/light
These properties make it useful in electronics and composite materials

nodes.label: Carbon nanotubes: cylindrical fullerenes with high length-to-diameter ratio
nodes.objective: Describe carbon nanotubes as cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios and their uses.
essentialPoints: Nanotubes are cylindrical fullerene structures
Very high length to diameter ratio
Useful in nanotechnology, electronics and materials due to strength and conductivity

nodes.label: Functional groups determine characteristic reactions of organic compounds
nodes.objective: Explain that a functional group is a specific group of atoms responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions of a compound.
essentialPoints: A functional group is a specific atom or group of atoms within a molecule
Compounds with the same functional group show similar characteristic reactions

nodes.label: Predicting reactions and reactivity from periodic table position
nodes.objective: Predict possible reactions and probable reactivity of elements based on their position in the periodic table.
essentialPoints: Elements' likely reactions and reactivity can be predicted from their group and period position
This relies on the shared outer-electron structure within groups

nodes.label: Metals and non-metals defined by ion formation
nodes.objective: Define metals and non-metals in terms of their tendency to form positive ions, and locate them on the periodic table.
essentialPoints: Metals are elements that react to form positive ions
Non-metals are elements that do not form positive ions
Metals are found to the left/bottom of the periodic table; non-metals to the right/top

nodes.label: Group 0: stable outer shells and lack of reactivity
nodes.objective: Explain why the noble gases are unreactive in terms of their stable outer-shell electron arrangements.
essentialPoints: Group 0 elements (noble gases) are unreactive and rarely form molecules
They have full/stable outer electron shells: 8 electrons, except helium which has 2

nodes.label: Early periodic tables based on atomic weight
nodes.objective: Describe how scientists before the discovery of subatomic particles classified elements by atomic weight, and the limitations of this approach.
essentialPoints: Before protons, neutrons and electrons were known, elements were ordered by atomic weight
Early tables were incomplete, and strict atomic-weight order sometimes placed elements in inappropriate groups

nodes.label: Recognising graphene and fullerenes from diagrams/descriptions of bonding and structure
nodes.objective: Recognise graphene and fullerenes (including nanotubes) from diagrams or descriptions of their structure.
essentialPoints: Identify single hexagonal sheet as graphene
Identify hollow spherical/cylindrical carbon cage structures as fullerenes/nanotubes

nodes.label: Examples of uses of fullerenes including carbon nanotubes
nodes.objective: Give examples of the uses of fullerenes, including carbon nanotubes.
essentialPoints: Fullerenes used for drug delivery, as catalysts, lubricants
Nanotubes used in electronics, reinforcing composite materials, nanotechnology

nodes.label: Combustion of alkenes: incomplete combustion and smoky flames
nodes.objective: Explain that alkenes burn with smoky flames in air due to incomplete combustion, unlike complete combustion of alkanes.
essentialPoints: Alkenes react with oxygen in combustion like other hydrocarbons
Alkenes tend to burn with smoky flames because of incomplete combustion
Incomplete combustion produces carbon (soot) as well as other products

nodes.label: Addition reactions of alkenes with hydrogen, water and halogens
nodes.objective: Describe the addition reactions and conditions for alkenes reacting with hydrogen, water and halogens, and draw displayed structural formulae of reactants and products.
essentialPoints: Addition reactions add atoms across the C=C double bond, converting it to a single bond
Hydrogenation: alkene + hydrogen (nickel catalyst) forms an alkane
Hydration: alkene + steam (acid catalyst, high temperature/pressure) forms an alcohol
Halogenation: alkene + halogen (room temperature) forms a dihaloalkane

nodes.label: Addition polymerisation: monomers, polymers and repeating units
nodes.objective: Describe addition polymerisation as many alkene monomers joining to form a polymer with a repeating unit matching the monomer's atoms, and draw diagrams representing this.
essentialPoints: Addition polymerisation is when many small alkene molecules (monomers) join together to form one large molecule (polymer)
No other molecule is formed in addition polymerisation
The repeating unit contains the same atoms as the monomer, with the C=C becoming a single C-C bond
Diagrams can represent the polymer formed from a given alkene monomer, and vice versa

nodes.label: Explaining metal/non-metal properties from atomic structure and position
nodes.objective: Explain the differing physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals in terms of their atomic structure and periodic table position.
essentialPoints: Metal/non-metal physical and chemical properties differ because of differences in atomic structure (outer electrons)
Reactions of elements relate to their electron arrangement and atomic number

nodes.label: Group 1 reactions with oxygen, chlorine and water
nodes.objective: Describe the reactions of the first three alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) with oxygen, chlorine and water.
essentialPoints: Alkali metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides
Alkali metals react with chlorine to form metal chlorides
Alkali metals react with water to form metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas, becoming more vigorous down the group

nodes.label: Group 7: nature of compounds formed with metals and non-metals
nodes.objective: Describe the nature of compounds formed when chlorine, bromine and iodine react with metals and non-metals.
essentialPoints: Halogens are non-metals existing as diatomic molecules (pairs of atoms)
Reaction of a halogen with a metal produces an ionic salt (metal halide)
Reaction of a halogen with a non-metal produces a molecular (covalent) compound

nodes.label: Group 0: boiling point trend down the group
nodes.objective: Describe and predict how boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass down the group.
essentialPoints: Boiling points of noble gases increase going down the group
This trend correlates with increasing relative atomic mass

nodes.label: Mendeleev's periodic table: gaps and predictions
nodes.objective: Describe how Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and altered atomic-weight order to fit properties, and how later discoveries and isotopes confirmed and refined his table.
essentialPoints: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements he believed were undiscovered
He sometimes reordered elements based on properties rather than strict atomic weight
Elements with Mendeleev's predicted properties were later discovered, filling the gaps
Knowledge of isotopes later explained remaining anomalies in atomic-weight order

nodes.label: Alcohols: functional group -OH and first four members
nodes.objective: Recognise alcohols by their -OH functional group and name/identify the first four members from formulae.
essentialPoints: Alcohols contain the functional group -OH
The first four alcohols are methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol

nodes.label: Using models to represent addition polymerisation
nodes.objective: Use physical or diagrammatic models to represent monomers joining into an addition polymer chain.
essentialPoints: Models can represent multiple monomer units linking to form a polymer chain
Models help visualise how the double bond opens to form single bonds linking units

nodes.label: Group 1: reactivity increases down the group
nodes.objective: Explain why reactivity of Group 1 elements increases going down the group, linked to outer-shell electron arrangement.
essentialPoints: Reactivity of alkali metals increases going down the group
Explained by the single outer electron becoming easier to lose as atomic radius increases and it is further from the nucleus

nodes.label: Group 7: trends in relative molecular mass, melting and boiling point
nodes.objective: Describe how relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point increase down Group 7.
essentialPoints: Further down Group 7, relative molecular mass increases
Melting point and boiling point both increase down the group

nodes.label: Reactions of alcohols: with sodium, combustion, dissolving in water, oxidation
nodes.objective: Describe what happens when alcohols react with sodium, burn in air, dissolve in water, and react with an oxidising agent.
essentialPoints: Alcohols react with sodium producing hydrogen gas and a metal alkoxide
Alcohols combust in air (complete combustion gives CO2 and water)
Alcohols dissolve in water to form neutral solutions
Alcohols are oxidised by an oxidising agent to form carboxylic acids

nodes.label: Fermentation of sugar solutions using yeast to produce ethanol
nodes.objective: Describe the conditions required for fermentation of sugar solutions using yeast to produce aqueous ethanol.
essentialPoints: Fermentation uses yeast to convert sugar solution into ethanol and carbon dioxide
Requires warm temperature (around 25-40°C) and anaerobic conditions

nodes.label: Transition metals compared with Group 1 elements
nodes.objective: Describe how transition metals differ from Group 1 metals in melting point, density, strength, hardness and reactivity, exemplified by Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu.
essentialPoints: Transition metals have higher melting points, densities, strength and hardness than Group 1 metals
Transition metals are much less reactive with oxygen, water and halogens than Group 1 metals
Examples: Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu

nodes.label: Group 7: reactivity decreases down the group
nodes.objective: Explain why reactivity of Group 7 elements decreases going down the group, linked to outer-shell electron arrangement.
essentialPoints: Reactivity of halogens decreases going down the group
Explained by increasing atomic radius making it harder to attract/gain an extra electron into the outer shell

nodes.label: Main uses of methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol
nodes.objective: Recall the main uses of the first four alcohols such as fuels and solvents.
essentialPoints: Alcohols are used as fuels
Alcohols are used as solvents (e.g. in inks, perfumes)
Ethanol is used in alcoholic drinks

nodes.label: Investigating reactions of alcohols
nodes.objective: Carry out practical investigation of alcohol reactions such as combustion or reaction with sodium.
essentialPoints: Safely react small quantities of alcohol with sodium and observe effervescence
Observe combustion of alcohols and compare flames

nodes.label: Carboxylic acids: functional group -COOH and first four members
nodes.objective: Recognise carboxylic acids by their -COOH functional group and name/identify the first four members from formulae.
essentialPoints: Carboxylic acids contain the functional group -COOH
The first four carboxylic acids are methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid

nodes.label: Typical properties of transition metals: variable ions, coloured compounds, catalysts
nodes.objective: Describe the typical properties of transition elements: forming ions with different charges, forming coloured compounds, and acting as catalysts, exemplified by Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu.
essentialPoints: Many transition elements form ions with different charges (variable oxidation states)
Transition element compounds are often coloured
Transition elements and their compounds are often useful as catalysts

nodes.label: Halogen displacement reactions
nodes.objective: Describe and explain how a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
essentialPoints: A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt
This demonstrates the reactivity trend down Group 7
Displacement is evidenced by a colour change in solution

nodes.label: Predicting group properties from electron arrangement and trends
nodes.objective: Predict properties of Group 0, 1 and 7 elements from given trends down each group, based on outer-shell electron arrangement.
essentialPoints: Properties of Group 0, 1 and 7 elements can be predicted from established trends down the group
Predictions are grounded in the shared outer-shell electron count within each group

nodes.label: Reactions of carboxylic acids: with carbonates, dissolving in water, reacting with alcohols
nodes.objective: Describe what happens when carboxylic acids react with carbonates, dissolve in water, and react with alcohols to form esters.
essentialPoints: Carboxylic acids react with carbonates to produce carbon dioxide, water and a salt
Carboxylic acids dissolve in water to produce acidic solutions
Carboxylic acids react with alcohols (with an acid catalyst) to produce esters and water, e.g. ethanoic acid + ethanol forms ethyl ethanoate

nodes.label: Carboxylic acids as weak acids: explanation via ionisation and pH (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain why carboxylic acids are weak acids in terms of partial ionisation in aqueous solution and the resulting pH, relative to strong acids.
essentialPoints: Carboxylic acids only partially ionise in aqueous solution, releasing few H+ ions
This makes them weak acids with a higher pH than a strong acid of the same concentration
This links to the general concept of strong vs weak acids and ionisation

nodes.label: Condensation polymerisation: two functional groups per monomer, small molecule loss (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain the basic principles of condensation polymerisation, involving monomers with two functional groups joining with loss of a small molecule such as water, using a diol and dicarboxylic acid example.
essentialPoints: Condensation polymerisation involves monomers with two functional groups each
Monomers join together, typically losing a small molecule such as water, forming condensation reactions
A diol (e.g. ethanediol) and a dicarboxylic acid (e.g. hexanedioic acid) can react to form a polyester
The repeating unit reflects both monomers linked by new bonds, unlike addition polymers

nodes.label: Investigating reactions of carboxylic acids
nodes.objective: Carry out practical investigation of carboxylic acid reactions such as with carbonates or forming esters.
essentialPoints: React carboxylic acids with carbonates and observe gas produced
Prepare a small sample of ester and note characteristic smell under safe conditions

nodes.label: Using models to represent condensation polymerisation
nodes.objective: Use physical or diagrammatic models to represent two different monomers joining with loss of small molecules to form a condensation polymer.
essentialPoints: Models can show two different monomers each with two functional groups linking together
Models illustrate the small molecule (e.g. water) released during each linkage

nodes.label: Amino acids and condensation polymerisation to form polypeptides/proteins (HT only)
nodes.objective: Explain that amino acids have two different functional groups and react by condensation polymerisation to form polypeptides, and that different amino acids combine to form proteins.
essentialPoints: Amino acids have two different functional groups in the same molecule (e.g. -NH2 and -COOH)
Amino acids react by condensation polymerisation to produce polypeptides
Different amino acids can combine in the same chain to produce proteins

nodes.label: DNA and other naturally occurring polymers
nodes.objective: Describe DNA as a polymer of nucleotide monomers forming a double helix, and name monomers of other naturally occurring polymers (proteins, starch, cellulose).
essentialPoints: DNA encodes genetic instructions and consists of two polymer chains made from four different nucleotide monomers in a double helix
Proteins are polymers made from amino acid monomers
Starch and cellulose are naturally occurring polymers made from sugar (glucose) monomers
